subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last Friday night, I was telling about the altogether deplorable unemployment situation in my constituency and in the whole Saguenay-Lake St. John area in general. Unemployment is so serious in my constituency over the whole neighbouring area that municipal authorities, local organizations, local boards of trade as well as the Saguenay-Lake St. John local of national unions felt alarmed about it and formed a "regional committee against unemployment", of which Dr. Henri Vaillancourt, mayor of the city of Jonquiere, is the distinguished president.
Last Wednesday, April IS, the representatives of that committee met with the premier of the province of Quebec and asked him to consider the number one problem of our region, unemployment. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, today is the premier's birthday and I want to join with his friends to extend to him my best wishes for a very happy birthday. Now that I have done my duty in the matter of etiquette, I shall go on with politics.
Mr. Speaker, I have never spoken in this house of what goes on in Quebec. However, because of the great significance of the matter for the unemployed in my riding and in the surrounding area, I think I have the duty and responsibility to refer to it today, at least with regard to the requests submitted to the premier and his answer to them.

The brief mentioned that at this moment there are in our area some 16,875 unemployed householders with dependents. It states too that a survey has shown that nearly 66,200 people, out of a total population of 250,000 are adversely affected by the lack of employment. The brief also points out that one of our householders is at present unemployed.
The committee members made several constructive suggestions to the premier. Now I know that those who volunteered to look into that serious matter in order to help the unemployed gave it much of their spare time.
Let me refer here only to those suggestions which might interest the federal government. In the first place the premier was asked- and I quote from the brief:
To see that Quebec is given an opportunity to avail itself of the federal government's offer in the matter of unemployment assistance and to accept Ottawa's co-operation in building access roads to mining areas.
For my part, I have repeatedly pointed out to this house that Quebec is the only one of Canada's ten provinces which is not participating in the unemployment assistance plan introduced in 1956 by a Liberal government. Of course, the chief weakness of the plan is the fact that it was adopted by a Liberal administration and by the very fact, is in violation of Quebec autonomy. Mr. Speaker, not only are the people of Quebec deprived of unemployment insurance benefits, but, through their income tax and other taxes of all kinds, they contribute to the payment of that special financial assistance which is being distributed in the nine other provinces of Canada, in order to help the unemployed who are not or have ceased to be entitled to unemployment insurance. It is not, as I said here previously, that I am jealous of my fellow citizens in other provinces who do enjoy those benefits, but I wish my fellow citizens from Quebec could recover at least a small part-however slight-of the hard-earned money they pay over to the federal government. That financial assistance would be particularly welcome at this time, in my area, because so many of our unemployed do not now get the benefits. Besides, we are very anxiously hoping the government will soon submit its proposed amendments to the unemployment insurance act, so that we might see whether it will give due consideration to the many unemployed who no longer get unemployment insurance benefits or will stop getting them as of May 15 next. What does the government propose to do for those people who will not qualify for unemployment
The Budget-Mr. Brassard insurance benefits next fall and next winter, and who are now out of work? Will the government evade the issue and tell us that unemployment is decreasing, or will it dare repeat to our faces, with all the cynicism and irony characteristic of certain government members, the words spoken to the Canadian people by the Prime Minister during an evening television broadcast on February 18, 1958, as reported in the Montreal Star of the following day, and I quote:
(Text):
"As long as I am Prime Minister of Canada," he said in a live telecast, "everything that can be done, everything without regard to limit, will be done to the end that no one shall suffer."
(Translation):
Everybody knows that, at the time during the last election campaign, the Prime Minister was speaking of the unemployment problem in Canada. That solemn declaration, that official commitment on the part of the first citizen of our country, if considered in the light of what is happening in Canada today, can only induce the people of Canada to lose faith in their public men. It is by dint of saying or promising something, and then not doing it at all or half-doing it, that public men end up by destroying the confidence the people had put in them. A great many people today look upon politics as a rather queer galley, and that is the very reason why many good men refuse to have anything to do with it. Should the situation deteriorate, it could, without the least possible doubt, lead to excesses that everyone would bitterly regret.
Mr. Speaker, in addition to asking the premier of Quebec to allow our province to enjoy the benefits of unemployment assistance, the representatives of municipalities and public bodies also urged him to accept co-operation with Ottawa with regard to the establishment of access roads to certain mining areas. This is another case where my fellow citizens from Quebec are paying for something enjoyed by other provinces, and this time something that does not bear the stigma of having been proposed by a Liberal administration. On behalf of a very large number of my constituents-the majority, I would say-I ask the government to confer with Quebec provincial authorities in order that my fellow citizens of Quebec may at least profit from a small fraction of the millions of dollars they are paying in taxes of all kinds to the federal government.

The Budget-Mr. Brassard
The Quebec premier's reply to the members of the local committee on unemployment assistance gave little cause tor hope; I would say it was similar to the reply made by the Prime Minister of Canada last fall to representatives of municipalities, when after a lengthy speech, he finally told them: "Go back to your homes, our commitments are too heavy". He did not seem to have called the conference to find a real solution to the many problems of municipalities, but rather for the purpose of keeping at least one of his many promises.
It was his own peculiar way of respecting the autonomy of municipalities which exist only by provincial government proxy and which, constitutionally, are unknown to the federal government. Those "daughters of the provinces", if I may use the expression of Quebec's premier, were standing there, shy and trusting before the Prime Minister of Canada, in the absence of any representative of their mothers, the provinces.
The premier of Quebec gave some of his reasons for his inability to do anything, then he seemed to seize the opportunity of aiming a shaft at his Quebec friends in Ottawa, as if he wanted to encourage them to speak his language here in this House of Commons. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, I would like to read out to you a paragraph-only the first paragraph-of the interview reported in the Toronto Globe and Mail of April 16, and I quote:
(Text):
Premier Duplessis moved one step closer to an open rift with the Diefenbaker government today when he charged that the new federal Conservative government has been no better than previous administrations in stealing Quebec's fiscal rights.
(Translation):
Such a statement, Mr. Speaker, may seem strange if compared to another declaration, that of the Hon. Antoine Rivard, as published in L'Evenement of March 21, 1958. The minister happened, entirely by chance, to attend a meeting of the federal Conservative candidate at Notre Dame des Lauren-tides, near Quebec. This is what he said:
"I am independent of federal parties, but I must be fair. And in all fairness, I must say that, in the past 10 months during which the Conservative party has been in power, we have advanced further in the recovery of our powers, in the protection of our freedoms and the defence of our rights, than during the 22 years of Liberal rule", said the hon. Antoine Rivard-
How can such contradiction be explained? Well, there is only one explanation: everything depends on timing, that is whether a speech is made before, during, or after an election.	*
Besides, this is also the present policy of the federal government. In fact, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) implicitly confirmed that approach when he stated, in a somewhat puerile speech, that after all election promises should not be taken too seriously. Another childlike statement which I should like to point out to the house is the one also made by the Minister of National Revenue in the same speech when he said, as recorded on page 2626 of Hansard:
If that disastrous event should come about, I am sure both the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister would be willing to start smoking cigarettes and drinking whisky to save the economy, but I think we need have no fear of such a catastrophe occurring-
I feel that such maturity of mind makes him fully competent to step into the shoes of the Minister of Finance. In any event, such statements made by the Prime Minister of Canada in this house are somewhat disappointing, coming from a man whose high office should raise him above party considerations. Why does he not leave such

The Budget-Mr. Brassard tasks to other Conservative members? There are some who are extremely well qualified in this field. To use an expression that is dear to the heart of the Prime Minister "the old glory of parliament" does not lie only in a bill on human rights, nor in a proposal for the abolition of the closure procedure, a matter which, incidentally, is no longer being mentioned.
The main point I wish to stress is that, during the period in which I served as a federal civil servant before being elected in 1957, I never heard the Right Hon. Mr. St.-Laurent cast personal aspersions on anyone who approached him, or try to humble them. His first and foremost interest was in directing the country's course.

speechtext:
As far as he was
concerned, the people of Canada always came before members or friends of the Liberal party; the interest of the country had precedence, and by a wide margin, over the interest of the party. He was at the same time head of the government and leader of the Liberal party, but he devoted 99 per cent of his time to the business of the country, occasionally accepting representational functions. He was devoted to his heavy administrative duties to such a point that he was criticized for not being enough of a politician. Even during election campaigns, he never indulged in extravagant promises just to get votes. He was a devotee of higher politics, the first citizen of the country, a statesman, maybe one of the most prominent and respected Canada ever knew. He did not make Canadians pay for his "vision" but just the same the whole nation benefited greatly from his greatness. He was not a man who considered only immediate results of the moment whenever he had to take a decision that could have important effects for Canadians; he would consider the whole area.
In 1955, just over six years after assuming the administration of our country, and after repeated invitations, he made his trip around the world. He was then 74 years old and indeed, it is not for the sake of pleasure or to avoid his task, and much less for the sake of publicity, that a man of his age undertakes such a tiring trip. So, his health was greatly affected by this exertion and I wonder if he ever completely recovered from the fatigues of that journey.
Wherever he went, thanks to his simple dignity, his poise, his skill, his modesty and


perfectly balanced judgment, he added great lustre to the reputation of this country, of which he was indeed the first citizen. If Canada now enjoys that enviable prestige all over the world, it is mostly due to the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent. It is also due, and certainly to no lesser extent, to that man who directed, with unmatched competence for nearly nine years, our Department of External Affairs, the hon. member for Algoma-East (Mr. Pearson), the leader of the Liberal party, who more than anyone else, in his functions, helped Canada attain, among the nations of the world, a rank held by very few countries of 17 million inhabitants.
It is precisely men of such mettle who are lacking in the Conservative party to direct our affairs today.
Precisely men like Right Hon. C. D. Howe, who is being criticized by many birdbrained people who do not know that Right Hon. C. D. Howe will occupy a select place in the gallery of the great builders of Canada. He had faults, I agree; he made mistakes, of course-political mistakes, I mean-but where is the serious and objective mind who will dare question his immeasurable contribution to the expansion and good administration of Canada during those twenty-two years in which he held office in successive Liberal administations? Besides, after his defeat, newspapers in the country were unanimous in paying tribute to the gigantic work he had done in those twenty-two years of political life, at the service of his fellow-Canadians. It is such a man, or men like him, I repeat, that the Conservative government urgently needs today.
The former Liberal team has been upbraided for having managed this country the way businessmen do, but, to say the least, in all that period which some fanatics still attempt to decry, Canadians knew where they were going, the country was sound and in good hands; nobody feared those chaotic business conditions that, today, brand as incompetent an administration playing at politics in a "mock parliament".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity to participate in this interesting debate. There are some who observe that the budget debate is not a very interesting performance. Sometimes the members of the press gallery indicate that, and occasionally even members of the house so intimate. Frequently, however, one notices the latter point of view emanating from those who do not participate in the debate!
The opportunity to congratulate the Minister of Finance is one which I welcome most heartily. He deserves great congratulations
The Budget-Mr. Macquarrie for the brilliancy and incisiveness of his splendid budget address and I believe, too, for the realistic appraisal of the economic state of the nation which he made some few nights ago. I believe that already his performance in this most onerous office in these most difficult times rates him with the great finance ministers of our nation's history, men like Fielding, Sir Thomas White and E. N. Rhodes.
The budget as the Minister of National Revenue pointed out, is perhaps a not overwhelmingly popular document, yet it is one that is being accepted realistically by the Canadian people. It is encouraging to note that it has won widespread approval from many economists in universities and various business bureaux, men who are specialists in the field of fiscal operations on the governmental level. There is a pretty general consensus that this type of budget was just the sort which was required for this particular phase in our nation's economic health.
I would be making no startling pronouncement if I said I am not one of those who rejoices over the contemplation of increased taxes, even the moderate increases that have been provided. But these are things which at this stage we must accept. It was Oliver Wendell Holmes who said some years ago that taxes are what we pay for civilized society. It seems we now live in a phase in our history, as my colleague the Minister of Fisheries pointed out the other day, when as the years go by the role of government in our daily life increases and, of course, as government grows the cost increases proportionately.
I am not one who is terribly alarmed about this development. I am not sold on the idea that the word "Conservative" and the word "reactionary" mean one and the same thing. I think if we look back on the history of Canada we will find that the extension of governmental operations dedicated to the welfare of the people has been carried on by parties of both labels which have held power in this country.
Looking over the program, projected and completed, of the government which I am proud to support, I see no place where I would suggest that a certain project or expenditure be blotted out or withdrawn. The programs that have been advanced in the interests of national development have served and will serve a very useful and valuable purpose not only in long range national development but, in the short run, in that important objective of cutting down the unemployment which the government faced early in its career for reasons that have been discussed many times in this house. The estimates, for instance, for the little province of Prince

The Budget-Mr. Macquarrie Edward Island, from which I come, are the largest on record. They represent assistance which will benefit directly or indirectly all the people of our province.
In considering questions of national development it is perhaps not surprising that I should focus my attention on one particular area, the maritime provinces. In the maritimes since our entry into confederation we have had many problems to deal with, many difficulties to surmount or at least to attempt to overcome. Some of these were imposed by geography, some by topography and some were aggravated and I am afraid augmented by confederation.
One of the most urgent of these, of course, is the problem of transportation. I suppose a railway timetable is not a usual reference paper in this house, but I should like to direct hon. members' attention to one little item which may graphically demonstrate some of the aspects of our transportation problems. If one looks at the railway timetable covering service between Ottawa and Montreal he finds therein that the railway lists a distance of 117.6 miles, and the Canadian National can make the trip in two hours. If he looks at the railway timetable for the run from the great railway centre of Moncton to the city of Charlottetown, the cradle of confederation, he will find that the railway lists a distance of 126.8 miles, and that the time for the trip from Moncton to Charlottetown is six hours and 20 minutes. Going the other way it is much faster; the trip is made in 6 hours and 5 minutes! I think that demonstrates graphically that we have a legitimate complaint when we make comparisons with respect to the transportation situation.
But one part of the trip from Moncton to Charlottetown is the water link between the province of New Brunswick and the province of Prince Edward Island, and I should like to devote some few minutes to that. Last week I made a short, quick trip to Prince Edward Island. On the way back on Thursday morning I encountered a situation which most certainly underlined for me the transportation problem that we in Prince Edward Island face. On arriving at the terminal at Borden, P.E.I. I found that no automobiles could be transported across the strait because that gallant old ferry, the Prince Edward Island, had suffered propeller trouble and was not able to leave the dock all day. Thanks to Maritime Central Airways, the one bright spot in the transportation system of the maritimes, I was able to get over to Moncton and back to Ottawa.
I must say that the officials of Canadian National Railways put forth their very best effort and the next day the Prince Edward Island was in operation again. On Thursday, the day the accident occurred, the ancient


ship Scotia was again brought into service and made some trips. But for some considerable time the province of Prince Edward Island was isolated as far as automobile traffic from the rest of Canada was concerned. This occurred because our No. 1 ferry, the Abegweit, was in drydock in Montreal for spring refit.
Three times in the last year the Prince Edward Island has suffered a complete breakdown and has not been able to operate on her usual run. Everyone knows that the No. 1 boat, the Abegweit, may at any time suffer some mechanical disability, as happens to any automobile, train or boat, and when that occurs the people of Prince Edward Island are dependent upon a very old boat which is displaying its inability to cope with the demands now being made upon it.
Down through the years this chamber has heard my predecessors from Queens and the predecessors of my colleagues from Prince Edward Island deal with the subject of communication between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. Indeed, as is known by all, Prince Edward Island was one of the colonies which were reluctant to enter confederation. For six years we demurred at becoming a part of confederated Canada. It was believed that the position of the province as an island isolated from the rest of the country and as a smaller province made for a different set of circumstances, and that our interests would not be altogether identical with those of the larger provinces to the west.
To mitigate against our separation and insularity great emphasis was placed upon the matter of communication. A situation was to be created whereby we would get all the benefits of a direct link with the Intercolonial and other railways which were being projected at the time. The disadvantages of our isolation were to be overcome, and on that basis the colony of Prince Edward Island entered confederation in 1873. The terms of our agreement are precise on this question, and I quote from the 1873 agreement:
The dominion government shall assume and defray the charges of efficient steam service for the conveyance of mails and passengers, to be established and maintained between the island and the mainland of Canada, winter and summer, thus placing the island in continuous communication with the Intercolonial Railway and the railway system of the Dominion.
I might say that last Thursday I found the communication neither efficient nor continuous! Down through the years there has been much dissatisfaction about the implementation of these terms, much hardship and, indeed, at times in the older days

actual suffering on the part of the people of my province in trying to make this connection with the rest of Canada. For years there was talk of a tunnel, and a survey was actually made during the administration of Sir John A. Macdonald. Boats were provided, but never did they seem to be adequate. In 1911 Mr. Robert Borden, leader of the Conservative party, came to the town of Summerside and said, "If you elect me prime minister of Canada you will get a car ferry." That promise was faithfully kept. The car ferry was built, and in his honour the terminal on Prince Edward Island was called Borden. This boat, built well over 40 years ago, is the one to which I made reference a moment ago. It has been crashing back and forth through the heavy ice of Northumberland strait for well over a generation. This splendid boat has been a credit to the fine Scottish shipyards which produced it, but it should have long since been put into an auxiliary role instead of being retained as one of the main links in this most important communication area.
There is still a feeling in the province of Prince Edward Island that we have not yet obtained the proper type of communication contact with the mainland. We do not talk about tunnels in this modern age but as this house has heard before we are very concerned, and very hopeful, that the final fulfilment of the confederation terms will be granted through the construction of a causeway which will provide continuous communication with the mainland. We rejoice that the government has taken such an interest in this project and has carried out such an extensive and, I believe, thorough survey of the whole problem connected with building the causeway.

speechtext:
I think there are many prospects in that connection, Mr. Speaker. We could, perhaps, make use of the names of a great many people who would be involved. Prince Edward Island would be very generous in the naming of it, if it emerged as an actuality. We look forward, in any event, to the tabling of the report on the causeway. It is our fervent hope that as a result of the report the government will have reason to believe that the project is feasible and will move forward to accomplish this final step in bringing this old island province into the kind of communication pattern for which it has sought so long.
I think I would not be guilty of excessive partisanship or of revealing a lack of realism if I were to say that this government has already demonstrated to Prince Edward Island
The Budget-Mr. Macquarrie an awareness of the needs of the island and a regard and consideration for its difficulties. This would lead one to believe that a government of this type, with a truly national view, would proceed to build a causeway for the province if it were technically feasible, to the advantage of the maritime region and Canada.
However, Mr. Speaker, I would not be covering this whole question if I stopped there. It would take some years, with the best engineering skill, to build that causeway. There is at this time an immediate problem, and important problem. We are hoping to see the causeway built, but I think this transportation situation at the present time has two important aspects. The first one is that the boat, the Prince Edward Island, is old and should have been replaced or augmented a good many years ago. The second aspect is that both the Prince Edward Island and the Abegweit cannot cope with the summer traffic which every year brings thousands and thousands of tourists to the beautiful province of Prince Edward Island. This indicates that there is much wisdom in every part of the world, very good judgment and taste. The demand for tourist accommodation is rising year by year. There is no place in which these tourists are more welcome than in Prince Edward Island.
We are very much concerned about the fact that we cannot get these people over fast enough, and that from time to time there are long lines of automobiles anxious to get across to the province. These boats now have to work under forced draft to accommodate these people. Until a causeway is built, if it is built and we hope it will be, immediate and interim action must be taken to provide another boat. Suggestions have been made to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) that this boat might be purchased outside of this country. I am not alone on this matter. All Prince Edward Island members are deeply concerned, thoroughly aware of the problem, and most anxious that the province's transportation be upgraded to meet modern conditions. I do not bring this problem forward as a humble suppliant for favours and certainly not in any posture of threat or club-wielding admonition. We in Prince Edward Island have scarcely the strength to take the latter position and certainly are not of the temperament to take the former.
On a basis of simple justice, as an appeal to the most helpful and understanding dominion government that Prince Edward Island has ever had, I put forward this case, just as my colleagues and I have in recent months to the minister concerned. We expect that our just cause will be fully and

The Budget-Mr. Macquarrie properly dealt with and that, as with the Borden government of old, the Diefenbaker government will move quickly and effectively to meet the vital needs of this great province of Prince Edward Island.
Mr. Speaker, there is a temptation for one to devote himself to matters concerning only his constituency. I was impressed with the remarks by the hon. member for Colchester-Hants (Mr. Kennedy) the other day when he spoke about his own reluctance to speak often, and then when I heard him describe the glories of Colchester-Hants I felt I was like him in that connection. Although the temptation is there, I should like to just direct a few thoughts to a subject which was discussed the other day by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Jung). He spoke about some of the economic aspects of Canada's position in the outside world. Certainly, I am not going to discuss such things as the Berlin crisis, which would not be appropriate at this time, and which I know are receiving attention of the ministry and absorbing the interest of all hon. members. There are two areas of what we might describe as external outreaching which I think that Canada, in its present position, might well explore a little farther.
I have been interested for some years in the Latin American area. In recent years Canada has strengthened its trade links with this part of the world. Recently new ties have developed in the West Indies federation. I know all members hope that these ties will be strengthened and relations will grow more friendly as the years progress. In this western hemisphere there is an old regional agency, the Organization of American states, which was founded in 1890. In the early days Canada could not become a member of this great body because we did not have jurisdiction over our foreign policies. Indeed, we would not have been too warmly welcomed by one of the great member nations immediately to the south.
But modern times have brought changed conditions and Canada is most heartily welcome at the present time. There is every evidence of that. I believe it would be a most valuable step, considering the present world conditions, if Canada moved to make complete the hemispheric solidarity in the western hemisphere and become a member of this very successful international organization, the organization of American states. We have much in common in the diplomatic field with its members, and I think our role could be not only a useful one but an important one, indeed perhaps great.
Then there is an area which today finds many changes coming in rapid succession. On the great continent of Africa we find that


the tide of nationalism rises faster today than it did in Asia, which event itself seemed to be just yesterday. In the United Nations we find that there are many new members about to enter that body. These come from the great and long-silent continent of Africa. I am sure we all remember that in our school days when we looked at the map of Africa we found if we wanted to trace the political status of certain areas we had to look at the map of Europe, where we could find the same colouring. Practically every part of Africa was a colonial state of some European country. In my school days there were only two independent countries, Ethiopia and Liberia, two small areas in a total continent of subjection and dependency. Yet now we find things changing, and changing very rapidly; indeed, so rapidly that there are political, social and economic ramifications of considerable disturbance. But these changes are bound to come. They are inevitable; they are irrepressible. The importance of these changes cannot be underestimated by a country like Canada which has been so successful in carrying its burden in world affairs and which has built up over the years such a fine reputation in the international field. I can but hope that Canada will move toward the realization of greater interest in this area and that our Department of External Affairs will expand in this part of the world and we will have more listening posts and greater awareness of this great continent, of its needs, of its interests, and of the burning desires of its people at the present time when they find themselves emerging into the field of national sovereignty and autonomy, with all its changes, responsibilities, difficulties and problems. I believe that Canada, with its great reservoir of goodwill and very fine staff of diplomats, in its splendid external affairs department, can do much to reach out to the peoples of Africa in these days when their disposition on questions of international diplomacy are of such great significance, and may tomorrow be even vital.
Perhaps with the great crises of international affairs which come upon us from day to day it is difficult to take a long range view. Certainly in these crises it is not so easy for Canada to play a commanding part, although we always, I hope, play an important one, but in some of these long range considerations I believe our role could be potentially greater perhaps than that we have yet played, thus enabling us to further the fine performance which we have to our credit.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I am sure that the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Marquarrie) will agree with me that it is desirable at the earliest moment possible for the government, through the Prime Minister

(Mr. Diefenbaker), to make an appointment in succession to the late and much respected secretary of state for external affairs. The hon. gentleman's interest in foreign affairs I know would justify my assuming that he would readily concur in this suggestion. The other day I addressed a question to the Prime Minister and asked him if he thought it was in the national interest to delay the appointment of a new secretary of state for external affairs until such time as all matters having to do with the budget had been completed in this house. The Prime Minister's irrelevant reply was interesting and is a matter of record, but it did not answer the question which I put to him. I therefore suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) that he might pass on to the Prime Minister the suggestion which I make on behalf of this group, that if the appointment of the new minister would be facilitated by this house dealing with all matters having to do with the budget at the earliest possible moment, he may be assured of that co-operation.
This is an all important matter, as the Minister of Finance, who sombrely looks at me now, will be the first to realize. This is a matter involving the appointment of the secretary of state for external affairs who will formulate, in co-operation with his colleagues, the foreign policy of this country at one of the most critical periods in recent history. We all admired, I am sure, the capacity and the competence of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) when he spoke for Canada at the recent anniversary meeting of the NATO council; but in following the precedents of other council meetings it would possibly have been helpful if other ministers had been present, particularly a minister charged with the responsibility of projecting foreign policy in this country.
The foreign ministers of the great powers are to meet soon. It may be that these meetings will be followed by a meeting at the summit. There certainly will be further NATO council meetings. This is one of the most important periods when Canada should not be without a secretary of state for external affairs. The President of the United States did not delay in the appointment of a secretary of state for foreign affairs in that country, and while the responsibilities of the government and the people of the United States are greater than the government and the people of Canada, this does not mean that our responsibility and our opportunity for constructive suggestion and participation does not exist. We hope, as I know the people of Canada hope, that there will be a decision in this matter by the Prime Minister at the earliest moment.
20, 1959
The Budget-Hon. Paul Martin
Mr. Speaker, this may or may not be the last budget of my hon. friend and classmate, the Minister of Finance. I can only say to him that because of my admiration for him, and my affection too, I sincerely hope that whatever he desires he will receive provided we are generally satisfied as to the competence which must attend the particular realization that he may or may not have in mind. I am sure that the Minister of Finance could discharge other obligations with great credit to himself and the country. I share with him the anxiety of these difficult moments until such time as this important decision will have been made one way or another.
I can only say to the Minister of Finance that, notwithstanding my goodwill toward him, like other hon. members 1 have an obligation to give some consideration to the budget which he presented to this nation a week ago last Thursday. It seems to me that the amendment offered so ably by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Beni-dickson) expresses in general terms our dis-satifaction and criticism of this budget, as I believe it now expresses the judgment and reaction of the people at large.
It proposed:
That all the words after the word "that" be deleted and the following be substituted therefor:
"this house regrets the bad faith of the government which sought and secured support from the Canadian people on a program of lower taxes, reduced expenditures and a balanced budget, and which has now produced, in flagrant disregard of pre-election promises, a budget calling for higher taxes, record expenditures and a large deficit."
This amendment is a criticism of the government for its reversal of the main elements of the Conservative party's financial policy as stated by the Minister of Finance and other spokesmen for that party in this house prior to the elections of 1957 and 1958. Now what were the basic elements in the former policy of the Conservative party as represented by the Minister of Finance and others? The elements of this policy were, first of all, balanced budgets, reduced taxes and a persistent effort toward the elimination of waste and extravagance. These elements were deeply imbedded in the policy of the Conservative party as stated by its spokesmen in this house. The spokesman for a long time was the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), the Minister without Portfolio in the present administration, and I have looked at some of the things that he had to say about financial policy. In Hansard, at pages 2764 and 2765 of April 5, 1955, here is what the financial critic of the Conservative

The Budget-Hon. Paul Martin party had to say about the matter of a deficit in a budget. He said on that occasion:
Now, deficits are things we should fully understand. We should realize what happens when we have a deficit; we should realize what it means. It means that the minister, after wringing out of us every dollar that he feels he can, after scraping the barrel, or rather the pocket, then goes out and borrows $194 million in order to keep level, and that means you and I and all the other taxpayers will have to pay that money back.
And then he went on, a little later-and this is the financial critic of the Conservative party speaking only a few years ago-to say:
We come now to the deficit, which is not a good thing. There is not a word to indicate any sense of uneasiness.
It seems to me that these words apply so aptly to the mood and to the demeanour of the Minister of Finance when he spoke the other night. The Minister without Portfolio, as he now is, continued:
There is not a suggestion that there is any chagrin. Certainly there is not a suggestion of any apology to the people of Canada. But after several years of booming times, of good times, they have not been able to organize the economy so people can get work. After all, in two general elections we were told that everything was going to be taken care of.
I have stated that the financial policy of the Conservative party was one of a balanced budget, and it is important, therefore, that we should have some idea what was the position of the Conservative party with regard to the question of surpluses. That statement by the financial critic of the Conservative party had to do with deficits, but the hon. gentleman also stated his views and those of his party on surpluses by quoting, as the minister will no doubt remember, from Mr. Snowden. Speaking on March 19, 1957, as reported at pages 2458 and 2459, the hon. member for Greenwood, then the financial critic of the Conservative party, had this to say:
This means that the government has taken an extra $382 million from the Canadian people. Philip Snowden used to say that if any government took half a crown more than it needed it was guilty of getting money under false pretences. But today the government has no hesitation in taking hundreds of millions extra from the taxpayer.
Now, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), though not dealing directly with this question of a balanced budget, said that if there had been a violation of Conservative party promises this was because of circumstances which existed unknown to the opposition. He suggested that the hon. members who presently sit on the ministerial benches did not know of a situation which the previous government had hidden from them. The conclusion reached in his observations was that if they had known this they would not have


made certain declarations or given certain assurances to the people of Canada, forgetting, of course, what the position of the Conservative party while in opposition had been, as stated by its financial critic and others including the present Prime Minister and, of course, the Minister of Finance whose observations are well known. But lest there be any misunderstanding about the position of the Prime Minister, the present leader of the Conservative party, long before this famous secret economic report of 1957, let us look at what the Prime Minister said in Saskatoon on June 13, 1953 as reported by the Star-Phoenix:
The Progressive Conservative policy was one of lower income taxes. There was no need to tax married men earning less than $3,000, particularly with the cost of living at its highest point in history.
And then at Clinton, on July 9, 1953, as reported in the London Free Press, the right hon. gentleman pledged an October session of parliament to cut taxes by $500 million, or $170 per family.
Then again, the Prime Minister is reported from Foxford on July 13, 1953 as having said, according to the Star-Phoenix that the Progressive Conservatives would remove the 10 per cent tax on such needs of the home as furniture, clothing, shoes, tea and coffee and other necessities now heavily taxed, and would provide for full taxation of all federal government properties on the same basis as was applied to all other municipal taxpayers.
And so it went on. And if there could be any doubt about the position taken by the leader of the Conservative party during the election, we now have the opportunity to examine a document which is well known to many hon. gentlemen but which I saw for the first time only within the course of the last few days.

I have no doubt that the Prime Minister has an interest in the average man and woman but I want to relate that interest to some of the things that he as leader of the Conservative party and the Minister of Finance and others told the Canadian people as a result of which they now sit to Mr. APRIL

Call a dominion-provincial conference for the purpose of making the Senate an effective arm of democracy.
We will discuss that at some other later date. I did not know that was in the party plank. But here is one that interested me very much because it has to do with what I have just been saying. This is the Prime Minister speaking:
Last year Canadians were over-taxed by $120 for every family of four.

Major elements increasing inflation are heavy government spending and high taxes in both of which fields the St. Laurent government seems to pride itself on its record of failing to reduce either or both.

A Progressive Conservative government will consider expanding the present old age pension system by the addition of an insurance system similar to that in the United States. The United States plan of old age and survivor insurance provides average monthly benefits on retirement of $76.00 for single workers, $128.00 for aged married couples without dependents and $65.00 for aged widows.
The average contribution per person is $27.08 not much more than the average contribution by Canadians of $22.70 for the old age pension. A Conservative government will consider implementing such a plan "in addition to'' the present pensions system. The United States plan is "worthy of the highest commendation."
Well, there will be ample opportunity to discuss that plan at some future date. There we have the Prime Minister promising to reduce taxes and increase benefits, not explaining how those contradictory things could be done. Supporting statements of a similar nature were made by every hon. member who now sits to Mr. Speaker's right and the overflow to Mr. Speaker's left as a result of which these hon. gentlemen sit in the seats of government today.

-tax changes to put Canadian companies on a basis of equality with foreign corporations or their subsidiaries operating in Canada.

-drastic changes in taxation treatment of oil companies.

Of course, these promises do not mean anything, we were told by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) who made a most unusual exposition, I thought, of a new theory of public morality when he said that commitments made to the Canadian people were not to be taken as seriously as commitments made by the Prime Minister or the leader of a party in this house.

The Minister of Finance is wagging his head in the negative but not too strongly. I suspect he thinks I am not quoting the Minister of National Revenue correctly. Let us see what that hon. gentleman did say as reported at page 2624 of Hansard of April 13, 1959:
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that promises of any kind, whether pre-election promises or otherwise should be honoured and resoected so

The Budget-Hon. Paul Martin far as circumstances will possibly permit, but I would suggest to you, sir-and I think all hon. members on both sides of the house would accept this general principle-that promises made to this House of Commons and promises made to parliament stand in an even more favoured position in so far as sanctity and respect are concerned than promises made during an election campaign.
I cannot say that this represents the view of the Prime Minister and I am sure it is not the view of the Minister of Finance, but I express the greatest surprise that the Minister of National Revenue, for whom I have always had the highest regard, should make that kind of distinction. Surely if public life means anything as we practise it in this country, an assurance given to the people of Canada is sacred whether it is made in this house or on the hustings during an election and made for the purpose, particularly during an election, of giving hon. gentlemen the right and the opportunity of governing the affairs of this nation. Assurances made to the people of Canada to cure unemployment, to cut taxes, to have balanced budgets and similar pledges cannot be dismissed unless we want to weaken the structure of our political system.
If the Minister of National Revenue does not fully concur in what I am saying I would ask him to look at the words of a great leader of the Conservative party and a former prime minister of this country, Sir Robert Borden who, speaking in the House of Commons on January 20, 1909, said:
I say that the system of offering bribes to the constituencies in this country is a vicious one, and that, so far as I am concerned, I lifted up my voice during the last parliament in favour of the prohibition by statute of such acts; and I hope some day to see this wrong righted in Canada by statute.
I looked up the Hansard of 1909 quite some time ago. I asked for it this morning in the library and it was not available. I would, however, refer hon. members to what Sir Robert Borden said which represents basically in principle what I have just said he did observe in this house on September 9, 1930, as reported at page 35 of Hansard of that date. At that page there appears a reference to the statement made by Sir Robert Borden on January 20, 1909.
Sir Robert Borden, leader of the Conservative party of that day, a prime minister of great note, felt that assurances given to the people of Canada were no different from assurances given in parliament by a leader of a political party and I say this by way of deduction from what he said. For the Minister of National Revenue to take a different position is, I suggest, to run counter to the kind of public morality that in this country most of our public men for a long period have sought to practise. As a matter of fact,


that this is the tradition is clear from what Professor Robert MacGregor Dawson the eminent Canadian political scientist says in his book, "The Government of Canada":
Election manifestoes are largely the work of respective party leaders and essentially personal pledges given by them to the electorate.
It cannot be otherwise construed or else the people of Canada would have the right to conclude that anything said by a leader in an election was not to be taken seriously. There would be nothing that would undermine our political system more than to find that what was said by the Minister of National Revenue in this house represented the true situation. I believe it does not. For that reason we have the responsibility and the duty of reminding this administration of the promises which it made in so many fields and with respect to a vast number of matters and particularly concerning matters relating to reduced taxation and balanced budgets.
As I have said, the Minister of Finance has broken all peacetime records by the deficit he announced in this house on budget night. His deficit for 1958-59, however, I suggest to him, is not as some other hon. members have indicated, not $617 million but $835 million. Every effort to conceal the true budget by accounting manipulation in the defence equipment account I suggest to my hon. friend was both improper and unconvincing. His use of the defence equipment account to finance expenditures for which he had asked approval was, I think, very misleading.
In that connection, I know what the Minister of National Revenue said about my estimate of a $1 billion deficit last year, an estimate which was based on suggestions that had been made by the Canadian tax foundation. The fact is-and I say this in reply to the Minister of National Revenue-that on the basis of the estimates submitted to this house last year the budgetary deficit would have been $950 million. Two things happened to reduce this deficit. First, as I just indicated, the use of the special defence account; and, second, increases in revenue. On the basis of the estimates submitted to parliament by the Minister of Finance the budgetary deficit, I say, would have been $950 million, since the expenditures authorized were $5,605 million, while the minister estimated revenues at $4,650 million. The budgetary expenditures, as finally estimated, amount to $5,387 million. The difference between this figure and the amount of $5,605 million is explained and accounted for by the fact, as I have noted, that the minister had used $218 million from the special defence account so as to make his budgetary expenditures appear less than they actually were.

This accounting device does not, however, change the fact, so that the actual deficit I say is $835 million and not $617 million as claimed by the minister.
But the minister took some pride in the fact that by this accounting device he was able to say that there was a deficit of only $617 million. Well do I remember the day when he rose in the house before he delivered the budget, without having previously gone through the usual courtesy of advising the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) of the figure which he proposed to give, and said that the deficit was not a billion dollars. He said, "Oh, no, my deficit is not a billion dollars; my deficit is not $800 million; my deficit is only $617 million," as though that in itself did not seriously reflect upon the financial policies of this government.
When my hon. friend took office in June of 1957 Mr. Harris had presented him and this nation with a budget which contained a surplus of $500 million at least, and now within 18 months-

speechtext:
When the Minister of Finance presented his budget he said little about the most serious problem that confronts Canada at this time. According to the bureau of statistics of my hon. friend, and not those of my own creation, when the minister delivered his budget there were 537,000 people out of work in Canada. In Britain there are 550,000 out of work. Canada, with a population of 17 million and a working force of 5J to 6 million has 537,000 out of work. Britain with a population of from 45 to 48 million with a working force of 22 million has 550,000 people out of work. Notwithstanding, these facts, the Minister of Finance, in a government which was going to see that no one suffered because of being out of work, had little to say in his budget about unemployment except that he looked for a recovery and an improvement.
He forecast an increase of 7 per cent in the gross national product. He did not

The Budget-Hon. Paul Martin indicate in his forecast how much of that would be as a result of a rise in prices. He certainly did not tell us that the 2 per cent increase last year or 95 per cent of it, was largely because of a rise in prices, nor did he tell us that if there is going to be a recovery, which we all certainly hope will take place, every indication, in so far as plant equipment is concerned, points to a continuation of a serious level of unemployment.
I ask the government, in the face of the situation that has confronted us this year, a situation that was allowed to arise in spite of our warnings last June and July, particularly those given by the Leader of the Opposition, to take preparatory steps now to meet a situation which we all trust will not be as serious as last fall and winter but which, in terms of unemployment, from most indications would seem to present this nation with a problem comparably as serious as that in the period we have just gone through. Now is the time for the government to anticipate that kind of a situation. I must say regretfully that from the statement of the Minister of Finance one would think that the situation was not one to be compared unfavourably with other western countries, that our situation was better than that in the United States, Sweden and other western countries. Of course this is not the case. There was very little reference to unemployment in the budget statement.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with real pleasure that I rise to take part in this debate and, of course, to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) on the realistic manner in which he has presented the budget. Truly it is difficult to analyse all the forces which contribute to our economic structure and if there has been some concern felt in the past we can gather encouragement from the inherent stability in our minister's purpose and from the cautious optimism of his forecasts.
Naturally we expect to find those who disagree but I believe sincerely that the government has made a tremendous effort to meet every challenge in solving our problems. Recently, in reading trade journals, financial forecasts and articles by responsible leaders of industry and finance, I have noticed that practically without exception they contain highly optimistic forecasts. These are the people who really know. They are planning their production and development to meet the needs they anticipate. Surely with the great expansion in industry and the development taking place all over the country today the value of our gross national product is bound to increase, and the Minister of Finance has indicated a figure which may prove to be very conservative.
Having dealt with expansion in generalities, may I say that I am fortunate enough to

witness in my own riding some of this industrial development which has been sadly lacking in the past in western Canada in general and Saskatchewan in particular. However, in keeping with the great development of natural resources in this country my constituency of Melville, which up to the present has been largely agricultural, will soon be playing a major role. In the southeastern part of the constituency, ten miles from the town of Esterhazy and 3,100 feet below the surface of the earth lie vast, untapped deposits of potash, probably richer in content and greater in abundance than any place else on earth.
In preparation for the removal of the potassium bearing ore, construction of the world's finest potash mine, to be operated by International Minerals and Chemical Corporation, commenced last year. The Utah Company of the Americas has the contract for this immense project, the cost of which will exceed $20 million. Development of the project has already brought an additional million dollar payroll to the area and there are further expectations for the future since 16 other companies are actively engaged in planning and exploration in the province. Surely this is an optimistic sign for further investment and development.
Areas such as I have mentioned are particularly fortunate, and while enterprises of the nature mentioned do stimulate the local economy the basic problems of agriculture still remain. While the farmer feels that the commodities that he sells do not bring him a return commensurate with what he has to pay for the goods he buys, he also has the added burden of increased costs for services, utilities and education. The only means local governments have of procuring revenue is from the taxation of real property and in the areas with which I am most vitally concerned taxes have more than doubled since the war while there has been a steady decrease in the prices of the farmers' primary products. The greatest costs have been those for education, which brings me to the point that there is a necessity for more consideration of the needs of education at the federal level.
Under the terms of the British North America Act education is solely a matter for provincial legislation. However, close to 100 years have passed since the B.N.A. Act came into being. With the passing of these years, times and conditions have changed to such an extent that some of our best educators are suggesting that the federal government should be giving consideration to the establishment of a federal department of education with a minister of the government at its head.
The Budget-Mr. Ormiston
The purpose of such a department would not be, of course, to take away any control of educational matters from the provinces but rather to assist in every way possible the existing provincial departments of education. I believe all political parties have acknowledged that the federal government has some responsibility for education but none has done too much about it. Quite possibly the reason for this lack of action is that no particular department or no particular individual has any definite responsibility for education.
Following the first world war the government of the day felt it should be doing more for education and, as a result, money was found for the establishment of technical schools in the larger cities across Canada. Then, education was promptly forgotten by the federal government until after the second world war when a federal-provincial agreement was drawn up to provide further technical education and the establishment of a number of composite schools across the country. This agreement has run its course and education has become dormant except in the minds of a few who are promoting its interests. Recently the great scientific advances made by the Russians have again stirred us to the point where we are giving more thought to advanced education.
It is suggested, that it would take something less than a world war or events of great significance to move us as a nation to thinking about education. The establishment of a federal department of education by the government would give official recognition to education. It would give us an official body with whom we could deal when making proposals about education. Up to the moment, no one has had any official status so far as education is concerned, and ideas about education have only been aired in this House of Commons.
A department of education such as I have mentioned could, among other things, do research in connection with education, even if that research were just to determine what the government's responsibility for education is. While the federal government's responsibility should extend to all levels of education, from elementary to university, a projected study by research personnel might come to other definite conclusions; in any event, such considerations should not be left to mere chance. Education merits intensive consideration by government and deserves something more than a passing opinion.
It is obvious that, especially in the rural areas of our country with sparse populations, any advances in education will be slow in coming if the financial burden is to be borne at the local level. It is true we have projects which will expand our industry and increase our population, thereby assisting in a great
2852	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Ormiston measure in distributing the burden of taxation. However, in the immediate future we must concentrate more on cutting costs than in promoting the ideas of "salvation by subsidy".
Whenever I think of cutting costs my thoughts invariably turn, in so far as agriculture is concerned, to our prairie port of Churchill which, with extended facilities, could do much more to produce a stable economy in the west. Even today prairie farmers save 12 cents per bushel on grain transported through Churchill and British buyers receive their purchases for 6J cents per bushel less via the Churchill route. However, it is unfortunate that of the 55 ships which visited Churchill last year practically all of them arrived in ballast. This, of course, offers some advantage in a quick turn around, but before any port can operate on a normal basis there must be at least some balance between import and export cargo. In so far as Churchill is concerned, the real difficulty is in finding a manner in which imports can be increased. The fact that so many ships arrived in ballast simply means that the Churchill hinterland is not importing from overseas. The area is not highly populated and naturally its buying power is limited. This condition may be attributed also to the fact that the purchasing habits are directed to other sources of supply.
In the west, as in other parts of Canada, our buying habits are influenced largely by the intense barrage of advertising propaganda directed at us through practically every medium of communication. This results in the demand by the consumer for goods from across the border being much greater than the demand for goods manufactured in Britain or continental Europe. However, it might be well to remember that only recently a contract was awarded in the United States to a British company bidding on a multimillion dollar project because the tender submitted underbid other competitors, largely from the United States, by $5 million. This is only used as an illustration, of course, to demonstrate that if price and quality are right, the supply which is nearest is not necessarily the best. Since it is not my intention to cast any unkind reflections on our neighbours to the south, or in any other direction, I think I might make progress in a somewhat different vein. (Translation):
Another type of progress is very evident in this house. I am referring to a simultaneous interpretation system, but I would point out that it is also a serious drawback. Several members who could be bilingual are limiting the extent and value of their contributions in this house by speaking only in


English. Let us hope that, in these times of great national unity, where there is greater cohesion among our members than any party has ever known, the results of this scientific age will not prevent these feelings of confidence and mutual understanding from being expressed verbally in both languages. (Text):
May I conclude, Mr. Speaker, on another note of progress which arises from events which have been taking place in my own constituency. I am able to draw the attention of the house to the "forward look" which is apparent in the Indian affairs branch of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. I refer to an important milestone which has been reached in the integration of the Indian into our modern society. Recently two treaty Indians were appointed to serve as assistant agents on the reserves in the File Hills-Qu'Appelle Indian agency. These appointments, I am sure, reflect the confidence of the department and its officials in the inherent capabilities of the Indians, and will act as an inspiration to other original Canadian citizens, as well as serving to prove that there are no strictions on ability and opportunity. May I suggest that these and other actions are further indications of the progressive nature of this government, and of the enterprise and initiatives of those devoted and able individuals who carry out its policies.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget introduced the other night by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) was something of an in-between budget. It was not a balanced budget, yet the forecast deficit was less than the forecast deficit of a year ago. It was a fence-sitting budget. It was a budget that was neither fish nor fowl and was directed mainly towards reducing the criticism in the press of this country without, at the same time, subjecting the Canadian people to the full tax burden necessary to bring about a balanced budget.
During this debate one is able to discuss a great many matters, and therefore I have the opportunity to refer to the same matter which was initially referred to this afternoon by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), namely the desirability of an immediate appointment to the post of minister of external affairs. There is disturbing news in today's press that United Kingdom Prime Minister, Right Hon. Harold Macmillan, in putting forward what I consider to be very important proposals which might have resulted in an easing of world tension, has been opposed by the United States, France and Germany. In this context I think it is more important than ever that Canada has at the earliest possible time a full time minister of external affairs, and that Canada should put

forward continuing proposals directed toward easing international tension. I am hopeful that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker), in the reply which he promised in the course of a few days in answer to a question of mine this afternoon, will support and strengthen the position taken by the prime minister of the United Kingdom.
This is no time in the history of the world to cling to inflexible positions which have been taken for many years. I believe, and the C.C.F. believe, that this is a time for negotiation, that this is a time for the putting forward of proposals directed at easing international tensions. I of course do not know who the Prime Minister may appoint to this very important portfolio, but I do hope that in considering the many able candidates, any one of whom might fulfil this post extremely well, the Prime Minister should not discount either youth or ability, that he should appoint the person who is likely to bring to this portfolio the best of judgment, tact and flexibility, keeping always in mind the necessity of achieving security and peace throughout the world.
I listened to the speech delivered by the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Ormiston) this afternoon, and I would like to say that I agree with his statement that the port of Churchill should be used to the greatest possible extent. This is a port which has assisted the economy of the prairie provinces. It is a port which is now just coming into its own. On the prairies we have been most happy to support the building of the St. Lawrence seaway, but in doing that and believing that it is in the best interests of this country, we submit that here also is a good case for an extension of and improvement in the storage facilities for grain at Churchill, and for greater use of this developing and important seaport.
We are now debating, Mr. Speaker, the amendment to this budget which was put forward by the official opposition. Basically we see in this debate at this time that there is little difference between the stand taken by the government and the stand taken by the official opposition. It has been said in the press that the budget debate lacks interest, that there has been little by way of keen debate. I think that is true, and the reason there has been so little interest taken in this debate is that the position of the Conservative party and the position of the Liberal party is almost identical.
