speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
All that the Liberal party has been able to do is to say to the Conservative party, "You haven't kept your promises." While they have been talking for a balanced
The Budget-Mr. Argue budget, I have not heard them criticizing the government for a deficit. I have yet to hear them say what steps they would take at this time to balance the budget. Mr. Speaker, I am not so much interested in whether the budget is balanced at this time as I am in having that kind of budget which will bring about the greatest amount of production in Canada and the very best possible distribution of that production.
This is not a forward looking budget. This is not a budget with a plan. This is not a budget that is designed to give leadership to the country to bring about full employment and maximum prosperity. This is a budget of tax increases. This is a budget with a sales tax increase. This is a budget which says to people who have had certain tax exemptions in the past when they were hospitalized, "Your taxes because of reduced exemption will be greater, and this increased revenue will help us bring the budget more nearly in balance."
This, Mr. Speaker, is the budget of a tired old party. The government has not been in office long but it is exhibiting the same characteristics as the former Liberal administration which had been in office for 22 years. This government is prepared to mark time, to leave it to the great corporations, to leave it to so-called private enterprise to see whether or not there will be greater production and a greater measure of prosperity in the years to come. There is a place in our nation for a political party that is a real alternative to either of the two tired old capitalist parties. We submit that although the word "socialism" has been greatly criticized in days gone by, the philosophy which we represent provides the only answer to the great challenges which confront Canada both internally and externally.
There should have been presented to this house a budget which provided for greater development and increased social services. This is not the time for a fence-sitting budget. This is the time for a budget of expansion. I would suggest that the government should have a special department devoted to economic planning and development. I would not ask that there be an additional minister. After all, with a large number of cabinet ministers, soon to be strengthened by an almost equally large number of parliamentary secretaries, there should be no need for another minister. There are two ministers who are marking time without any portfolio, also the Secretary of State and the Solicitor General, both of whom I am certain are doing a very good job, are under-employed. There could be an amalgamation of these portfolios and thus the opportunity to provide
2854	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Argue a new department of government which would look to the expansion of this country.
Is there something that should be done now to provide for full employment? I would think so. The statistics with regard to unemployment are still disturbing. The Minister of Finance, in the best forecast he could make, did not predict anything approaching full employment. I suggest that one of the first things that should be done is to bring forward a greatly expanded winter works program which would provide opportunities for employment next winter when seasonal unemployment is likely to be on the increase. The C.C.F. believe in full employment at all times, but we realize that it is more difficult to provide employment in the winter time. Now is the time for planning; now is the time for consultation; now is the time for discussions with the provinces so that this useful program can be greatly extended so as to remove as far as may be possible seasonal unemployment.
The Minister of Finance has himself indicated that the budget does not provide for special accounting for capital funds, and I would suggest that there should be a separation of the main fields of expenditure into two general accounts, and that there should be a large capital fund established for the purpose of capital expansion. This fund, amounting, I suggest, to $2 billion, could be used by the government whenever it seemed necessary and desirable to supplement and complement private investment so as to assure full employment and greater prosperity in this country. There is plenty of scope for increases in capital works.
Another thing which such a department as I have proposed-a department of planning and development-should be doing is to survey the road and highway needs of this country. The government has clung to the single road policy of the former administration, namely the trans-Canada highway. This government should not be satisfied with maintaining that program; it should provide a program of co-operation with the provinces in order to construct a second trans-Canada highway, to build other main highways running north and south and, in short, to supply a modern highway system for this country. Such a program could not be considered as a hand-out or as frivolous expenditure. This would be a project which would return great dividends to the Canadian people in years to come.
There is another area of social investment which is crying out for action, and that is the field of education to which reference has already been made this afternoon. We are faced with a need for more schools, the


need for increased facilities at our universities and the need for capital assistance toward the building of educational institutions all across the country. I wish to commend expenditures such as this to hon. members and I submit that they constitute important uses to which a capital expansion fund could be put.
There is another important field of capital expansion which needs attention, and that is the provision of increased hospital facilities across our nation. It is true that the government and previous governments have been providing some money for hospital construction and expansion, but the amounts have been far too small. In addition to general hospitals, there is an urgent need for the expansion of hospitals designed to take care of the mentally sick people in our nation. Here is another important field of social investment which requires action at this time.
However it appears that the government intends to mark time for the next 12 months. This is a '-stand pat" budget-a status quo budget. In the submission of the C.C.F. group we should have a budget which would increase the productive facilities of our nation. I have never been one who has advocated government ownership merely for the sake of government ownership, but I do believe that public ownership has an increasingly important role to play in a modern society. The possibilities of public ownership have never been developed in this country as they should have been. Here is an area for expansion which if developed would greatly improve the standards of life in our nation.
No matter what has been stated to the contrary, the C.C.F. believes very much in private ownership of private property, the private ownership of small business, the private ownership of certain industries which are in fact, competitive and where the exploitation of employees does not exist. We also believe in supporting co-operative ownership, and in this respect I hope that the government will consider bringing to parliament a national co-operative act such as is being requested by the co-operative union and other co-operative organizations across this country. We think that co-operative ownership is one of the very best methods of ownership at any time. It is democratic ownership; it enables people to bring together large amounts of capital in order to do the jobs that only large amounts of capital are capable of doing, and at the same time it enables them to do this on a democratic basis and to return the profits, or

savings as they are usually termed, to the consumer or to the producer as the case may be.
The next form of ownership is corporate ownership which is very rapidly developing in our nation into monopoly ownership. We see the means of production in this country accumulating steadily in the hands of fewer and fewer people. We see one large industry after another concentrated either in a single company or in the hands of very few companies, and it is to offset this type of monopoly ownership that we suggest it is the duty of government to develop public ownership and co-operative ownership.
I think there are important fields where public ownership should be extended. For example, we should like to see future trans-Canada pipe lines, either for gas or oil, publicly owned. Indeed, we believe that the pipe lines now belonging to the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Company should be brought under public ownership. We say that national trans-Canada pipe lines which are, in fact, a natural monopoly should be publicly owned. We feel, also, that the steel industry which, we submit, stands in need of great expansion in this country, is a field in which public ownership might be very appropriately developed. This is not to say that some segment of the present steel industry would not lend itself to public ownership, but certainly here is a place for some measure of public ownership in the future development of this industry.
The fertilizer, drug and chemical industries are more and more under monopoly control. Here is a place where the development of public ownership would, we believe, bring about a reduction in the price of the commodity to the consumers and make a good return on investment to our nation.
There are other areas in which public ownership could be usefully developed. We submit that although the Conservative and Liberal parties have turned their backs on public ownership and have in general opposed any expansion in this field, if our nation is to meet the challenges of unemployment, greater competition in export trade and the general challenges of the twentieth century, then the field of public ownership should be greatly expanded.
There is another area in which we feel there is room for the development of public ownership and that is in the field of credit. Interest rates in this country are becoming alarmingly high. The exorbitant interest rates that are being allowed and promoted by this government will endanger expansion and constitute such a serious threat that the trend toward expansion may be being reversed.
66968-9-182
The Budget-Mr. Argue I have spoken on other occasions in this house advocating a great reduction in certain interest rates and in certain controls. I believe the chartered banks in this country are doing an abominable job as far as developing loans in the small loans field is concerned and with respect to providing loans to people with low incomes. This has resulted in a great explosion of activity by small loans companies, moneylenders and loan sharks, as I call them. Although this government may wish the chartered banks in Canada to develop the field of small loans there is no indication that it does and even if there were there is no guarantee that the chartered banks would do that. Many of them apparently are quite happy to take the easy business that comes to them without having to bother with a large number of small loans. They merely pick off a few easy and lucrative loans in this field.
I suggest that we have here a field where public ownership could be developed. I do not intend to suggest that the federal government should immediately socialize the chartered banks but in all sincerity I say to the Minister of Finance that here is a wonderful opportunity for those who say they believe in competition and free enterprise to go to the chartered banks and give them a chance to compete by establishing in this field a publicly owned system under which small loans could be made by chartered banks.
I concede that the previous administration and other governments in the past have come close to this by one means and another. There has been established an industrial development bank for intermediate credit. A system of publicly owned chartered banks would provide credit at low cost to prospective borrowers and would provide real competition in this field for the chartered banks.
The policy of high interest and tight money followed by this government is just as badly conceived and is just as great a detriment to Canada and its national welfare as it was when it was inaugurated by the former administration. I do not always agree with the remarks of the Minister of Finance but I did concur in the strong statements he used to make condemning the former government for allowing the Bank of Canada interest rate to go higher and higher and in condemning the previous administration for its so-called tight money policy.
We now have a Conservative, high interest rate, government. This is a government that is saddling the ordinary people of this country through their private borrowings- and the municipalities and provincial governments along with them-with unnecessarily high interest rates. It is time this ill-conceived policy was reversed and I suggest
2856	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Argue that public ownership is one means of bringing about the desired reversal.
There is another field in which public ownership might be developed. As a matter of fact, I notice that some of the great corporations of this country are now beginning to say there is a need for some central credit organization to which they could go to obtain long term credit in order to compete in international trade with the Soviet union and eastern bloc countries. Here is an opportunity not just for an export-import credit insurance act which we now have and which guarantees loans made from the banks, but for a public organization with public funds which could ensure that Canada has an opportunity to expand her exports and to increase her overall trade.
Our trade is reaching a real crisis. Although we develop or expand new markets from time to time we soon find them in serious jeopardy because trade is so greatly unbalanced. In 1957 Poland purchased from us over $16 million worth of goods. In that year, we purchased from Poland just over $1 million worth of goods. In 1958 trade with Poland almost ceased. In 1958 we exported to the Soviet union almost $9 million worth of products and in the same year we imported from that country less than $6 million worth of products. We should not be surprised that the present trade negotiations with Poland and Russia are encountering great difficulties, not because these countries do not wish to purchase from us but because our trade is so greatly unbalanced. I believe these countries stand ready to purchase from us at least in volumes equal to their purchases in the past if we would buy from them.
I suggest that an international trade bank or trade organization be established with funds available to carry on a government program established by a department concerned with national development to bring about expanded trade and a much better balance of trade. These are some of the ways through which we could expand the productive capacity of our nation.
In expanding our productive capacity we should not overlook the need for a great advance in social security and welfare measures. At no time should we complacently say that we have gone far enough, that our old age pension is as high as it should be or that our health program is satisfactory. Instead we should develop and improve these programs year by year. I suggest that action should be taken this session to bring about a contributory system of old age pensions on a much higher level than at present and related to recent annual income. The C.C.F. program in this field is


well developed. We feel that such a program should carry with it a basic old age pension of not less than $75 a month and a contributory program providing pensions above that amount.	[DOT]
Some hon. members may throw up their hands in horror and say that this is a program the nation cannot afford. I can remember former ministers of finance telling us that old age pension programs, family allowance programs and health insurance schemes are not a real burden on the nation in the sense of expenditures for war or defence but rather are basically transferred payments for certain well defined social services.
I submit we can afford these services and I submit that this kind of improved services would be a beneficial investment for our nation. As a parliament we owe it to our elderly citizens to act to improve their income. This government promised action. What did we get? We got two voluminous volumes of the Clark report. You can go through that report with a fine tooth comb or a magnifying glass and you will not find on which side of the fence Dr. Clark stands, whether he is for an improvement in our system now, related to the system in the United States, or whether he thinks we have gone far enough.
I imagine it is just the kind of report that this government wanted; it is a report of confusion; it is a report without any exactness; and it is a report that will enable this government, if it wishes, to delay, to procrastinate and to forget its very important promise to the Canadian people.
We of the C.C.F. for many years have advocated a system of national health insurance. We are pleased that in recent years there has been some progress toward this end. As a member of the C.C.F. party I am very proud that the province of Saskatchewan, as far back as 1947, pioneered the field of public hospitalization in our country, not without difficulties, not without many problems. But with all of those problems we in Saskatchewan have developed a pattern for hospitalization that has been copied and is being copied both in Canada and in the United States.

I would suggest that now is the time for a further great advancement in the field of health. Now is the time to bring into our health program, medical and dental coverage. government is making for the present insurance program covering expenses. But by going to hospital one incurs only a part of the expenses which are brought on because of ill health. This is no time for a fence-sitting budget, Mr. Speaker; this is no time for this inbetween, stand-pat budget, and this is no time to listen to nor to follow the suggestions and the criticisms of the official opposition because theirs has been a negative approach. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the old days before the building of the lighthouses, the poor noddies of many a Newfoundland outport prayed for wrecks-aye, and with easy consciences. Only the few hundreds of them who took to deep sea voyaging in those days had any awareness of the outside world, or of its people. All the world, excepting their own outports, was either down north or up along. It was a grand, rich place where all men wore shirts and collars each day of the week and ate pure figgy-dufls. The folk up along, therefore, had the easy end of life and why should they not contribute something of their goods and gear to the honest Atlantic province's noddies?
In those days they used to say the wrecker's prayer, which hon. members will find, if they care to consult it again, in the Penguin volume of Canadian verse at page 109. I shall quote only a few verses from it before resuming my debate. The wrecker's prayer went like this:
Give us a wrack or two, good Lard,
For winter in Tops'il Tickle bes hard,
Wid grey frost creepin's like mortal sin And perishin' lack of bread in the bln.
66968-9-182J
The Budget-Mr. Morris
A grand rich wrack, us do humbly pray, Busted abroad at the break o' day
An' hove clear in 'crost Tops'il Reef,
Wid victuals an' gear to beguile our grief.
God of reefs an' tides an' sky,
Heed Ye our need an' hark to our cry!
Bread by the bag an' beef by the cask,
Ease for sore bellies bes all we ask.
One grand wrack-or maybe two?-
Wid gear an' victuals to see us through
Til spring starts up like the leap of day An' the fish strike back into Tops'il Bay.
One rich wrack-for Thy hand bes strong!
A barque or a brig from up along
Bemused by Thy twisty tides, O Lard!
For winter in Tops'il Tickle bes bard.
Loud an' long will us sing Yer praise,
Marciful Fadder, O Ancient of Days,
Master of fog an' tide an' reef!
Heave us a wrack to beguile our grief.
Many previous members of parliament have spoken in this chamber, Mr. Speaker, of the disabilities which the Atlantic provinces have incurred since confederation. Many speakers have asked in effect that the government of the day "Heave us a wrack to beguile our grief". Recently the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, in a series of ten editorial comments, pointed out some of the disabilities of the Atlantic region and suggested some possible cures. I have not the time in this debate to discuss this series of editorials in detail and I therefore took the liberty a few moments ago of placing a collection of these editorials in the boxes of hon. members at the House of Commons post office. In summary the recommendations, which were the result of considered editorial concern, can be broken down into six. The first was special tax concessions, either in the form of tax holidays or in the form of accelerated depreciation allowances, the latter not as attractive to us in the east because accelerated depreciation is only of benefit to those firms already operating at a profit.
The second major step would be a revision of the national freight rate structure to end the pattern of present horizontal per ton mile rate increases. In this regard there is a growing sentiment in the Atlantic provinces that we do not really want a national freight rate policy if that national policy means one policy right across the country. What we want in the Atlantic provinces is a national freight rate policy composed of separate regional policies, for what will do the job for other regions will not do the job for us.
The third recommendation of the editors of the Halifax Chronicle-Herald was special low rate capital loans. In this regard it is noteworthy that the United Kingdom government now has in operation a Distribution

The Budget-Mr. Morris of Industries Act which provides for low rate, long term capital loans to establish industries of benefit to the entire nation in those areas of the nation which have not in the past prospered from industrial expansion.
Fourth, the newspaper believed that special federal consideration should be given to the building of new highways and water transportation facilities. In this regard I believe that the Atlantic provinces members generally accept the proposition that the first phase of the trans-Canada highway project should be pursued with continuing vigour to completion on schedule but that it should then, and only then, be succeeded by a subsequent phase of highway development which we feel should take into account the incapacity of the Atlantic provinces to share fully on the present sharing basis. I have in mind that the province of Newfoundland finds it difficult to finance its share, and consideration should continue to be given to the possibility of equating its contribution to highway construction with that of other Canadians. In my province we shall continue to hope and to press that in the subsequent phase of the trans-Canada highway some of our larger centres now omitted in phase one, notably my own city of Halifax, will be linked to the trans-Canada highway to provide that freight may be moved by highway and thus contribute salutary effects on competitive transport charges and so that other Canadians may come to us and we may go to other Canadians.
The newspaper also advocated greater regional allocation of defence and other contracts for publicly financed undertakings. I shall have more to say about that in a few moments.
Finally, it advocated increased attention to certain sections of the United States tariff program having to do with the importation into that country of such unrefined Canadian resources as gypsum which is now shipped in bulk from my province for subsequent processing in the United States, therefore producing less prosperity for us than it might otherwise do.
In considering any budget speech, Mr. Speaker, we in this house are sometimes bound to be animated not only by partisan considerations but by regional considerations. In this regard it will be of interest to hon. members to recall the final report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, better known as the Gordon economic report. I want to say quite frankly that I am one of those who in the heat of election campaigns misused this report. The report has suffered a bad fate because it has been said sometimes that all it recommended for the maritime
provinces was the deportation of our skilled workers. Now that I am able to contemplate the report with more consideration, there is much more in it than simply sloughing it off for that one unfortunate wording. At page 404 of the final report the authors of the report state as follows:
An objective of economic policy should be to integrate and improve the basic economic framework of the Atlantic region, including in particular the transportation facilities of the area with a view to facilitating and encouraging economic growth within the region. This is not likely to be accomplished by a multiplicity of uncoordinated measures providing aid on an ad hoc basis.
It is this point, Mr. Speaker, which I shall try to expand in greater detail following the supper recess. It is in essence that we in the Atlantic provinces would like to see an early end to hand-out government. We want to be regarded as being Canadians on our own feet. We do not want to have to pray, sir, "good Lard, heave us a wrack."
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a new spirit of buoyancy in the Atlantic provinces, a spirit of optimism that at long last we are, in the east, moving away from being backbenchers in a family of Canadian equals. We do not want to continue indefinitely in the Atlantic provinces living in an economy in which our livelihoods depend upon handouts from government. In the words of the premier of Nova Scotia, the Hon. Robert Stanfield-if I may borrow a phrase from that distinguished parliamentarian the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill); one of the really great Canadians of our time-we have been busy in Nova Scotia, too busy bailing to fix the boat. We want to stop bailing and get at the job of basic reform.
What do we hear from the opposition spokesmen, both in this house and in the local legislatures? Their hope for the Atlantic provinces continues to exist in the dream of the wreckers, "Give us a wrack or two, good Lard, For winter in Tops'il Tickle bes hard."
Everything is black, everything is wrong in the maritime provinces. It is not part of my business to advise hon. members of the opposition why it is they lost the election and will stay where they now are, but as long as they are out of tune with the youthful, vigorous, viable and vital optimism of the people of the maritimes and preach only wreckage, they will consistently stay out of touch with the thinking of the people. We know what it is to be backbenchers in the Canadian family. We want an end of it. There is a great deal of lip service paid to Canadianism and national unity. We believe in national unity. We maritimers were here when Canada was born. We want to be equals and we want to do a basic job of reforming our economy and not live by continued handouts.
The Budget-Mr. Morris
I quote from the Ottawa correspondent of the Times of London, who wrote in that distinguished world newspaper after a visit to the Atlantic area:
There is an unmistakable atmosphere of hope, much of it engendered by the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council, coupled with a determination to fight against the tide of depression. This is particularly evident among the younger generation. They do not want their provinces to be perpetually responsible to federal aid as a bolster to their economy.
Mr. Speaker, I have the opportunity in this budget debate to address myself to only three specific subjects having to do with the economic well-being of the peoples of the Atlantic area. The first of these has to do with the impact of the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway upon us and upon the use of Atlantic ports. I am bound by the rules of this house not to address myself to a debate which takes place in the other place. I am not free to debate what has or is about to be said in the other chamber. I know, however, that on this Wednesday the other place is to debate a resolution having to do with the impact of the St. Lawrence seaway upon the ports of Halifax and Saint John.
Statements which have been made outside that assembly by the principal architects of this resolution indicate that they have only recently discovered that the St. Lawrence seaway will have an impact upon the Atlantic coast area. One of these two gentlemen is a former member for Halifax and the other is a former premier of Nova Scotia. On Wednesday they will debate this resolution, within two and one-half days of the first cargo moving through the St. Lawrence seaway. They now discover the seaway will have an effect on Halifax and Saint John.
After 90 years of waiting, and only 60 hours from the opening of the seaway, what are we told by them? We are told that the St. Lawrence seaway will cause a loss of business to the ports of Halifax and Saint John. We are told this by people who had the responsibility of putting forward that view when, in fact, they supported the federal administration of the day, indeed one of them as premier of Nova Scotia. However, not a word was uttered, not a word passed their lips, not a word from the lips of the surviving Liberal members in this house. I have been here since October, 1957 and I have not heard one Liberal member from the Atlantic area- there are precious few of them left-say a word about the St. Lawrence seaway. Why is this so? It is because they were committed to it by the last government. It was commenced by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), who I regret to note is not in his seat tonight. He started it; it was his

The Budget-Mr. Morris idea as minister of transport to put it through, and after having conceived it as a member of the cabinet he quit that job and moved into the seaway authority to make sure it got built. Then he moved back into politics, expecting a different result from that which accrued in June, 1957.
I will pass over this. The vicissitudes of political life come to young and old alike. He not only moved back and forth between a position of governmental responsibility and that of functionary in charge of construction, Mr. Speaker, but when he left he left the further construction of the seaway in the hands of a gentleman who is now the executive vice-president of the national Liberal federation. So we have a definite Liberal policy of building the seaway. All right, Mr. Speaker; the young sentiment in the east is not opposed to the St. Lawrence seaway because we do not feel we can seek to acquire greater justice for our people by denying it to others. Lest anybody think in other places that this is a discovery, two and one-half days before the opening of the seaway, which is now going to have a deleterious effect upon us, let me say these very people are the people who had the capacity to be meaningful in their representations to the government.
Mr. Speaker, what is the Liberal policy as regards transport through the St. Lawrence seaway? That policy was conceived by the hon. member for Laurier as minister of transport and then as head of the St. Lawrence seaway authority. But he is not satisfied. Nobody in the back benches of the Liberal party speaks about this in the house, only in the other place. But here we have to be beatified by public awareness every four or five years. On January 21, 1959 the hon. member for Laurier expanded the Liberal transportation policy in the St. Lawrence basin. He was not satisfied to put the seaway through and to build it. He now has another plan, and you will not hear about this in the other place. At page 155 of Hansard of January 21, 1959, asked by the government to give some idea of things which he might undertake to improve the economy he said:
The first is for the immediate appointment of a board of engineers for the purpose of studying and reporting upon the economic advantages of linking the St. Lawrence river with the port of New York via the Richelieu river, lake Champlain and the Hudson river.
Then the hon. member went on to say that he wished he had time to go into the matter more fully, and we all wish he had had more time. Then he went on:
All I can say at this time is this: If it were given consideration and put into effect by a recommendation, of course following a report of

a board of engineers, it would put to work thousands of people in an area where work is required.
Certainly it would put into employment thousands of people. Here we have a seaway which has been paid for by the taxes of all Canadians. The hon. member for Laurier initiated the seaway and put it through. Its first cargo will go through on Saturday, as the Toronto Telegram says, meaningfully enough "a cargo of politicians." We have already had enunciated for us a new Liberal transport policy. Now we are going to dig a ditch between Montreal and New York. This would mean the complete eradication of Atlantic coast ports.
I draw the attention of the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) to the fact that when I spoke in the house last year I mentioned some quotations he had used in connection with regional projects. He asked me at that time where I had got these quotations. I said that I was paraphrasing, and he said, "If you must paraphrase, paraphrase accurately." Well, it turned out I was paraphasing accurately, and I have come tonight with the quotations. The Fredericton Gleaner of March 19, 1958, just twelve days before the election, quoted the hon. Leader of the Opposition as saying that "a policy of scattered, unco-ordinated projects would create jealousy harmful to national unity." The Montreal Star of March 18, 1958, quoted him as saying that regional projects create "regional jealousies which could affect Canadian unity." Mr. Speaker, at a time when the St.Lawrence seaway is about to come into operation for the benefit, as we in the east hope, of all Canadians, although we have our fears, for the Liberal party to now come along and advocate that we divert everything travelling east from Montreal south to New York, most of it through United States territory, is that not a regional project likely to create strains on national unity? I suggest that the hon. Leader of the Opposition get into the habit of sending copies of his speeches to his seatmate so that both of them know what each other is saying.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not doubt that the hon. member quoted me quite correctly, of course, but I would ask if he objects to this kind of canal junction between the St. Lawrence and New York through Quebec province? Would he object to that?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, absolutely, until the St. Lawrence seaway is reasonably well paid for. I have, as do many of my constituents, the highest respect for the hon. Leader of the Opposition. In fact, we think he is too good

to lead the bunch he does lead, but he is at perfect liberty to preside over a group of prayerful wreckers. He may smile at my answer, but it is more meaningful than some answers I have heard from the Liberal side of the house. I oppose the suggestion absolutely until the seaway is reasonably well paid for.
I would now like to give the hon. members of the house some idea of the antecedents to that opposition. Mr. Speaker, on September 12, 1864 a large dinner was held in the former Halifax Hotel in Halifax. The decision to advance to confederation was not taken in Charlottetown but in Halifax; but thereby hangs another tale. I doubt whether hon. members opposite consult the Creighton study of Sir John A. Macdonald, but if they do they will find the story there. At that meeting Sir Georges Etienne Cartier said this:
I have heard since I have been in Halifax the objection thrown out that there is much danger that you would be absorbed. It will be very easy for me to dispel such fears. I answer them by a question: Have you any objection to be absorbed by commerce? Halifax, through the Intercolonial railroad will be the recipient of trade which now benefits Portland, Boston and New York ... It is as evident as the sun shines at noon that when the Intercolonial railway is built-* and it must necessarily be built if confederation takes place-the consequence will be that between Halifax and Liverpool there will be steamers almost daily leaving and arriving at the former-in fact it will be a ferry between Halifax and Liverpool.
The Hon. George Brown said:
But far in advance of all other advantages would be this, that union of all the provinces would break down all trade barriers between us, and throw open at once to all a combined market of four millions of people. You in the east would send us your fish and your coals and your West India produce, while we would send you in return the flour and the grain and the meats you now buy in Boston and New York.
Sir John A. Macdonald said:
What will be the consequence to this city, prosperous as it is, from that communication? . . . Build this road and Halifax will soon become one of the great emporiums of the world. All the great resources of the west will come over the immense railways of Canada to the bosom of your harbour.
Let us be bipartisan in this series of promises to the Atlantic ports. Let us quote a Liberal prime minister, the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who moved in the House of Commons on July 30, 1903 for leave to introduce a bill for the construction of a national transcontinental railway. On page 7671 of Hansard of that date he is reported as having said:
Let me observe that if we have used American ports, it is not because for five months in the year our own ports are ice-bound. Everybody knows that our ports in winter are just as open as the American harbours. Everybody knows that if we
The Budget-Mr. Morris have used American ports and the bonding privilege, it was not because our harbours were icebound in winter, but simply because we had no railways to reach them.
I should like to cite chapter 71 of the acts of 1903 authorizing aid in the construction of a railroad, and sections 42, 43 and 45. I should also like to cite section 13 of the acts of 1911, chapter 6; chapter 20 of the acts of 1914, section 6, and section 21 of chapter 29 of the statutes of 1955, the last of which says:
The board of directors of the Canadian National Railways shall so direct, provide and procure that all freight destined for export by sea that is consigned within Canada for carriage to National Railways either at point of origin or between that and the sea shall, unless it has been by its shippers specifically routed otherwise, be exported through Canadian seaports.
I draw the attention of the house to the ordering "shall" rather than the permissive "may", and I should like the government to give consideration to the manner in which the C.N.R. is complying with the statutory conditions and the earlier statutory citations all of which, I am advised, are still in force.
We in the Atlantic area have changed from an attitude of defeatism to one of buoyancy and optimism. We still have hard problems ahead, but we have had much experience in the handling of hard problems. I have here Thursday's edition of the Halifax Chronicle-Herald with the headline: "Record Investment for Atlantic Area this Year". This points out that the value of this year's investment spending in the Atlantic provinces will be increased by 10 per cent over spending last year despite the fact that the national investment intentions appear to be slightly lower than last year. In this regard it is interesting to note that in the investment intentions the manufacturing sector is particularly hopeful and that there are indications of a three-fold increase over 1958. Indeed, an accompanying statement from the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council says this indicates that "investors are aware of the manufacturing opportunities in the Atlantic provinces and are determined to take advantage of those opportunities by spending large sums to enlarge present enterprises and to establish new ones."
Despite all this, from both groups of the opposition we hear nothing but despondency and gloom. Nothing but gloom. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), another hon. member who is not in his seat tonight, has a solution for our seaway problems which may suggest itself to the hon. member for Laurier. The hon. member for Assiniboia possesses, not only knowledge about how to solve all problems but he has a solution before the problems even arise. Prior to

The Budget-Mr. Morris the announcement of St. Lawrence seaway tolls he said: I want to say this-not for myself, and not on behalf of the members of my group in the house, but for the C.C.F. party-that we are opposed to all tolls on the seaway. He wanted no tolls at all. Taxes would be taken from British Columbia and taxes would be taken from Newfoundland, but there would be no tolls on the seaway. And this is from a group in the house which is now composed almost entirely of agrarian protesters and former employees of the international woodworkers association. These are all that exist, but they have a solution for everything. I have said here on a previous occasion that if the hon. member for Assin-iboia were asked to express his opinion in connection with the international regulation of space I believe he would say: I cannot tell you exactly what form it will take, but it will not work unless you have deficiency payments.
We have now in this house two opposition groups, one of them dedicated to constructing yet another channel for diverting trade through United States ports, the other to no tolls. Hon. members will recall that on August 29, 1958, as reported in Hansard on pages 4311, 4312 and 4313, I showed that the total amount of exports of Canadian products leaving this country via United States ports for overseas destinations amounted to $154 million a year and that imports entering Canada from overseas points for Canadian destinations amounted to $239 million a year. And yet some hon. members wonder why the Atlantic provinces area has sometimes had to pray the good Lord to give us a wreck. It cannot be denied that our ports and our facilities have not been used to anything like the extent of which they are capable.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, may I speak briefly about one of the things which we in the Atlantic area think we can do, if it is to be done, as well and perhaps better than anybody else in the country? The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) paid our area a visit during the latter part of last week, and he announced in Halifax that if there was any contemplation of an atomic submarine program we would build the submarines in Canada, not for appearance's sake or for the sake of prestige but in terms of useability. This is a reasonable argument. Maritimers are well aware of what is to be said in favour of things being done on the basis of serviceability rather than prestige. I note there has been a subsequent announcement by a Montreal firm in this connection saying that they were prepared to go ahead with this work. But this is one job which Atlantic companies believe, with all respect, they can do better than anybody else. We build ships, and we have built


them for longer than other people. The Halifax Shipyards Limited, a division of A. V. Roe which is lineally directly related to Hawker Siddeley, the only United Kingdom firm now building nuclear submarines, is closer to more of the Royal Canadian Navy than any other shipyard; two-thirds of the ships and the officers and men are based on the Atlantic command at Halifax. This shipyard knows more than any other Canadian shipyard about the construction of atomic submarines or other vessels.
I say this because I am one of those who believe that Atlantic provinces rehabilitation depends in part at least upon the people themselves. We must not come here as whiners. We must come here prepared to exercise our own initiative and not only to point out our disabilities but to suggest ways in which they can be corrected. It has been estimated by competent economists that the lower level of economic activity in the Atlantic provinces area costs this country $300 million a year. No Canadian saves anything by subsidizing the maritimes. It will be better to help us up to our feet and let us make our own way.
One final word more, and I have finished. It has to do with Newfoundland. I am not the one and this is not the place to comment upon the recent controversies that have raged in the headlines between members of the federal government and the premier of Newfoundland but because I am a member from the Atlantic provinces-

I thank hon. members of the house and particularly hon. members of the opposition for that courtesy. I will not trespass long upon it. I simply wanted to say that hon. members from the Atlantic provinces are perhaps, because of geographic propinquity, more acutely aware of Newfoundland than are other hon. members of this house. While I do not feel that I am the one or that this is the time for comment upon recent controversies involving the federal government and the premier of Newfoundland I do say this. I believe and my people believe that the government of this country should rotate only between the Conservative and Liberal parties and not between

those parties and the socialists. There is this bond of affection between us. We believe that government exists for people, not people for government, and underlying all the controversies are the people of Newfoundland themselves and their disabilities. If they have disabilities I am the lesser as a fellow Canadian and I therefore suggest for the earnest consideration of the premier of Newfoundland that in this tenth anniversary year of confederation of his province with Canada he consider the efficacy of inviting a tripartisan group of parliamentarians to his province so we could effectively discharge our duties to the people of Newfoundland, which are as great but no greater than our duties to all other Canadians.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as is customary during the budget debate we have heard speeches on a variety of subjects. I, however, would like to address myself to a subject that either by design or by accident has been scrupulously avoided by the members of the government in particular. The press of our country has made it no secret that it cannot understand why parliament and its members have not in any way at all debated the resignation of Commissioner Nicholson of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
As recently as two days ago on the national television program "Viewpoint", Mr. Blair Fraser, the alert and knowledgeable political observer-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A good Grit.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will quote Conservatives as well because this is an impartial subject unless it be that hon. gentlemen opposite have already prejudged that it is not an impartial subject. I shall quote sources of all kinds because I believe it is a matter affecting every hon. member of this house regardless of where he sits.
As I was about to state, Mr. Fraser remarked that he considers Commissioner Nicholson's resignation one of the most important items before parliament. He expressed astonishment at the fact that not a word has yet been said about it during the present budget debate. A similar opinion was expressed as far back as March 19 by the Ottawa Citizen which published an article under a three-column headline entitled, "Members Strangely Silent on Nicholson Resignation." Permit me to read the two brief opening paragraphs of this article:
The strangest thing about the resignation of Royal Canadian Mounted Police Commissioner Leonard Nicholson is the virtual silence that has reigned in Ottawa since it was announced on Monday.
The Budget-Mr. Crestohl
Members of all political parties seem unhappy that he quit but nobody seems anxious to talk about it or to try and blow it up into an issue.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: So you are going to do it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, I shall not do it. Your party probably will be the one to make an issue of it. I am trying to suppress an issue.
At this stage, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to discuss directly the cause of the resignation itself but I consider it an act of the greatest importance to parliament and indeed to the country when a top civil servant of the standing of the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police suddenly resigns because, as he himself has put it, he had no option and, as Mr. Maurice Jefferies of the Windsor Daily Star described it in the March 17 issue, he resigned in protest.
I believe that parliament has been and is delinquent in remaining so strangely silent during all this time. Not only should we have debated the matter long before today but I consider it was our duty to probe much further into the cause of this resignation and the reasons that lay behind it. We should know just what the commissioner meant when he said he resigned because he had no option. What did the commissioner mean when he said he resigned in protest? What was it he resigned in protest against? Why should parliament remain silent in the face of these two statements made by the commissioner? I believe they are vital to the very existence of our security. The simple announcement of the resignation by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) is not sufficient. The resignation came as a distressing surprise to the house and indeed to the entire country. Because of the unusual suddenness of this event I had expected that the government would have at once and of its own volition set up a probe to inquire into the background of this vital matter.
The government is the only authority that has the power to establish an inquiry and ferret out the reasons for this resignation. Much to my surprise and certainly to the surprise of the entire country as evidenced by the press the government allowed the significance of this event to lapse into the background. Obviously the government is quite anxious for this issue to remain in the background. I fear that unfortunately many painful implications can flow from the unexpected resignation of any of our top civil servants and particularly that of the chief of the organization which is responsible for the internal security of the country.
When a resignation results from normal retirement or perhaps from illness or incapacity, it could be a sad event but when a
2864	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Crestohl man resigns in the prime of his life with many more useful years of valuable and important service to give to his country and when in fact his resignation involves even a personal sacrifice we are definitely remiss in our duty if we do not explore to the utmost the reasons for such a resignation. In this particular case especially parliament should be concerned. The commissioner had a very high record and he said in his resignation he had but one more year to complete in order to be entitled to his full pension but nevertheless he sacrificed the advantages of that and resigned.
He would not normally resign under those circumstances or under circumstances which touched the interest and security of everyone in Canada. Nevertheless, he says he is constrained to resign, and he explains why he was unable to follow the course indicated by the Minister of Justice, with which he could not agree and which he apparently found to be inconsistent with his sense of duty. For an attitude such as this a civil servant deserves to be applauded by all Canadians. This is an exemplary form of behaviour, and it maintains the high standard of all our civil servants.
As I see it, it is the duty of parliament to protect and to safeguard the integrity of all our civil servants, especially those at the top who carry the burdens of responsibility. Moreover, it is the duty of parliament to sustain their independence. We must not expose them to any form of partisan pressure or influence at any time. We must hold inviolate their courage to discharge their duties regardless of the change of government or regardless of the change of a minister. Parliament has frequently applauded the fearlessness with which the Auditor General of Canada, for example, submits his reports and his recommendations. He has always been courageous and at times, Mr. Speaker, even daring in the frankness of the observations which he makes in his annual report to parliament and in his testimony when he appears before parliamentary committees, be it the committee on estimates or the committee on public accounts. I am sure that everyone in this house, and indeed the entire country, recognize and appreciate this independence of our Auditor General.
In the same category of top civil servants and their staffs for whom parliament must or should preserve the same freedom and independence, and who must be liberated from any anxiety which often follows a change of government, I would include all our deputy ministers, the chairman of the civil service commission, the chairman of the national research council, the chairmen of all similar commissions and councils, the


governor of the Bank of Canada, the presidents of all crown corporations and most certainly, Mr. Speaker, the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. We must spare them apprehension of how they might be affected by any change of government or by any change of a minister.

speechtext: Like 1935.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not speaking of 1935; I am speaking of 1959, and you will soon hear why.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member is the last one who should be talking about 1935 to 1945.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, that lesson was learned in 1930 when the Conservative government came into power and we saw what happened. We realized the independence which we must preserve for our civil servants. I say, Mr. Speaker, we must relieve them of what might sometimes be terrorizing fears which can come from the fact, to use a biblical phrase, that there arose a new king in Egypt who knew not Joseph. I suppose if the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) were here he would say to himself he wished he were that king who did not know Joseph. The civil servant has a continuing responsibility and this responsibility must not be shaken by any change of government or political pressure, since the duties of civil servants must be discharged with the courage and impartiality which are characteristic of honest civil servants in contrast with those who for selfish reasons seek to curry favour with a new government or with a new minister.
Let me illustrate what I mean, Mr. Speaker. We heard a typical clarification of this entire problem in the house on April 15 last week. I refer to a speech delivered by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Nasserden), and I quote from page 2729 of Hansard. This is what the hon. member said:
I think this government-
He was referring to the present government.
-has been entirely too generous with many of the people in the public service of Canada who do not appreciate that there has been a change of government. Some of these people still think that orders come from Liberal headquarters.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am very pleased to hear that he is not the only one in the government party who still thinks that way and who still supports that statement.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The facts are there.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The facts are there? Let us look at the facts. What does the hon. gentleman mean when he says that the government is too generous with the civil servants? Does that generosity consist in the fact that they are not dismissed from their employment? In what does the generosity of the government consist toward the civil servants of Canada? Is that meant to be a subtle threat to all the civil servants who worked for this country before this government came into power or what else does the reference mean? What does the hon. member mean, for example, when he says that the civil servants do not appreciate that there has been a change of government? How does he want the civil servants to manifest their appreciation?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: By being loyal.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does he expect them to fall on their knees twice a day and sing hallelujahs for the new Prime Minister and the new government? Is that how these gentlemen would like to have the civil servants show their appreciation?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If you do not know why are you drawing conclusions?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Just be patient. I do not know, nobody has said or indicated.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are trying to insinuate things.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Nobody has indicated how the civil servants can show their humility, their appreciation, their thanks and their gratitude for being permitted to serve the country as they have done in the past. I should like to know also what the hon. gentleman means when he says:
Some of these people still think that orders come from Liberal headquarters.
Where does the hon. member or the government think orders should come from? Should they come from the Conservative headquarters. I say, that this is an issue that is not without some difficulty for civil servants. Their integrity must be maintained; their independence must be protected, and we should liberate them from such thoughts as were expressed by the hon. member for Rosthern and as indicated also by other hon. members in the government. I am sure, that the members of the government want that independence for all civil servants and it is to this matter that I am addressing myself.
I consider, Mr. Speaker, that the remarks of the hon. member for Rosthern are an undeserved and unwarranted reflection on the honesty and integrity of our civil servants. As I have indicated, it is precisely this and similar thinking against which we must protect our civil servants. Just look at what
The Budget-Mr. Crestohl happened in the house today. To me it was a very shocking thing. When the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) asked a question of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough) the Speaker ruled that the question was not framed

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It was out
of order.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will tell you what it was. Just wait and listen. The Speaker ruled

I agree with the Speaker's ruling if that will satisfy my friend-that the question was not framed in accordance with our standing orders. That is perfectly true, and the question was ruled out of order by the Speaker quite properly. But here is what I say happened. An accusation was read by the hon. member for Fort William and I should like to read it again. As found in the Toronto Telegram of April 16, it reads:
They charged that the order was drafted by the pro-Liberal civil servants merely to embarrass the government while Prime Minister Diefenbaker was absent.
The minister sat in her place, having read the accusation levelled against her employees -whether or not it is true is immaterial for the moment-saying that pro-Liberal civil servants drafted the regulation in order to embarrass the government. I respectfully submit that the minister should not have waited for a question to be asked. It is my submission that the moment she learned there was such an item in the press she should have risen in her place on a question of privilege and vigorously denied the accusation against civil servants in her department. Her failure to rise in her place and deny an accusation against old and tried civil servants is to me quite disturbing.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are you trying to create a sacred cow?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I cannot hear the hon. member.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are you trying to create a body above criticism or reproach?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am making no accusation against the minister. I am making no accusation against civil servants. If the hon. member will follow me he will realize I am trying to point out that here was an occasion when the integrity of civil servants should have been upheld. The minister should have stood up in her place and said, "No, I will not permit this; I deny vigorously that my employees wrote this order in order to embarrass the government. That is not true." That is what I expected her to say. However, she

The Budget-Mr. Crestohl remained silent. This is something which supports the thesis I am trying to present this evening to hon. members.
When I referred a few moments ago to the importance of preserving the courage, integrity and honesty of our civil servants I must say that, without reflecting on any of them at all, I place the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in a category by himself.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will tell you why. He above everyone else must be free from and unfettered by any political fears and influences.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Should he decide policy too?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member who interrupted me may not feel that he should be free from and unfettered by political influence but certainly there is no one else in the entire country who will agree with him. 'On the contrary, the people will agree with my statement. When there is interference, when attempts are made to encroach upon the independence of the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, every Canadian, every member of the house and every person elsewhere in the country is placed in jeopardy and our democratic institutions become weakened and exposed to danger. I therefore urge that because of the possibility, or even the slightest suspicion that someone in authority has, because of political expediency, attempted to disturb the great confidence which the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police has always enjoyed-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What political expediency?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I said if there is the slightest suspicion it is a responsible duty of parliament to call on the government to dispel this suspicion and to set up as speedily as possible an objective and impartial inquiry into the matter. If there is nothing to be afraid of, why object to it, why oppose it? Why not go along with it?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why defend it?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not defending it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What are you doing?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am saying "if there is suspicion." The hon. member has not paid attention. The commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police resigns suddenly at personal sacrifice and hon. members opposite are willing to sit by and say that they are not interested as to why.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How do you resign gradually?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The country is far more disturbed by the possibility of such interference than can be readily imagined. The impartiality and independence of the force which gives Canada its internal security must not be left in doubt. Let me indicate from only a few press editorials the degree to which this agitates and disturbs the entire country. I should like to read a brief opening paragraph from the Fundy Fisherman of March 25, 1959:
Canada has lost one of its most distinguished public servants in the resignation from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police of Commissioner L. H. Nicholson. This outstanding son of New Brunswick refused to allow the R.C.M.P. to be made use of to further the ends of political expediency. He chose the sterner path of duty, and resigned when it became clear that he would not be allowed to maintain law and order in the manner and form required by the oath of his office. He will be honoured by people across the country and his example will be applauded by citizens of his native province.
I should also like to read an excerpt from an editorial in the Edmonton Journal, the other end of the country.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about British Columbia?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am glad hon. members have caught the mistake. It was not intended at all. This editorial appeared in the issue of March 20, 1959, and reads in part as follows:
However, a larger question has been opened by justice minister Fulton's grave decision to interfere directly with the movements of the R.C.M.P. This question concerns the degree of political control over the police possible today. It deserves the serious consideration of parliament.
Further, Mr. Speaker, in an editorial in the Ottawa Citizen of March 17, 1959, headed "Commissioner Nicholson Resigns" I find the following:
The resignation of Commissioner L. H. Nicholson from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police raises questions of policy in the administration of the R.C.M.P. which deserve the most searching inquiry. In recent days, the cabinet has evidently gone over Commissioner Nicholson's head, on one occasion countermanding an order he had given, and on the other giving an order of which he knew nothing. In his own words, this made his position untenable.
The result can only be confusion and some loss of morale in the R.C.M.P., which has had to meet enough difficulties in the past few days without this added trouble.
Another editorial, Mr. Speaker, appeared in the Financial Post of March 21, 1959, entitled, "The Man of Principle."
Decent people everywhere instinctively respect the man of principle, and particularly the man who is willing to suffer because of his principles.
Such a man is Commissioner L. H. Nicholson of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, just resigned-

Nicholson was a conspicuous success in one of our country's toughest and loneliest jobs.
His decision to do what he believed to be right -without regard for the present government's popularity with the labour vote-ends a career in a way that brings lustre to him and to the finest traditions of the public service.
From these expressions of public opinion across Canada, it is clear that the country wants to know whether or not there has been political interference or political overtones which provoked Commissioner Nicholson's resignation. What the country wants to know is just that, and it is the duty of parliament to set up an inquiry to ferret out the truth so that the country may retain its confidence in our civil servants.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would the hon. member
permit a question?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does the hon. member feel that ministers of the crown are duty bound, under all circumstances, to accept without question the recommendations of senior civil servants?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I cannot answer that question, but I certainly believe that the refusal to accept a civil servant's direction-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Direction?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -or suggestions, has its consequences with the top civil servants.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You do not know what you are talking about.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This is something that you do not want to hear, but the country wants to hear about it. You will hear from the country when the country is told the facts. I feel that the inquiry which I suggest should be promptly set up. I cannot understand why there should be the slightest hesitancy to set up this inquiry. I cannot understand fears that anyone should have about setting it up, because the confidence of the top civil servants has been badly shaken and it should be restored.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is the most unmitigated nonsense I have ever heard in the House of Commons.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am very much interested in hearing all these objections. I suggest an inquiry be set up in order to explain all the facts relating to this occurrence which shook the confidence of the entire civil service.
Commissioner Nicholson refused to be budged from what he saw his duty to be, notwithstanding any ingenious methods and specious arguments that were presented. I say, therefore, that one cannot help but admire Commissioner Nicholson all the more
The Budget-Mr. Crestohl for stating in his letter to the Minister of Justice, so frankly and so fearlessly, the following and I now quote:
I realize that other issues are before you which arose from this strike, but I feel most strongly that the matter of law enforcement should be isolated and dealt with on its own merits.
I underscore the words "on its own merits", Mr. Speaker. Then, he continues, and I quote:
This is the attitude the force has taken throughout. It has not concerned itself with the issues back of the strike, but has merely tried to maintain law and order in the area.
It appears that this is what the commissioner was desirous of doing; nothing more and nothing less. However, when he felt that his duty was being interfered with he took, as he himself describes it, the only course open to him. He resigned. I am sure the entire country will say to him, "Bravo". By his action he has sustained, if not even elevated, the high standards and traditions of this distinguished force for its courage and integrity, for which it is world renowned.
I respectfully urge the government to recognize this exemplary civil servant and not permit him to suffer, amongst other things, any financial loss because he did his duty with courage and with honour to himself and to the reputation of the men under his command. A most appropriate editorial on this subject appeared in the Montreal Star of March 18, 1959, which, in my opinion, effectively makes an appropriate recommendation to the government. I desire to read it into Hansard. It is entitled, "Colonel Nicholson Deserves well of his Country" and reads:
In his graceful tribute to Commissioner Nicholson, expressed in the correspondence surrounding the sending of R.C.M.P. reinforcements to Newfoundland, the Minister of Justice wrote: "You can rest assured that whatever may be the views as to the present situation, you have earned the respect and esteem of all those with whom you have served."
This respect and esteem is in no sense diminished by the fact that Commissioner Nicholson has disagreed with his minister and resigned on an issue of principle. It took courage to do this at a moment of public controversy. It took courage to do this more particularly because Commissioner Nicholson is within a year of his normal retirement from the R.C.M.P. after completing a full term of service. That service has been distinguished by a devotion to duty and a concern for the dignity and effectiveness of the force against a background of tradition that has made it a symbol of law enforcement tempered with mercy the world over.
It would be anomalous in the circumstances if Commissioner Nicholson should suffer a disability of any kind by reason of his resignation on grounds of principle. If his resignation is accepted now he will in fact suffer a financial disability. His pension will be lower than it would be if he completed his full term of service a year hence.

The Budget-Mr. Crestohl
A grateful Canadian people would support a move to grant him leave of absence for a year, when he could retire in the normal course on full pension. Such a course is commended to the government.
If this were the appropriate time or if it were possible for me now or at any other time to move a resolution to that effect or to introduce a bill to that effect, I would not hesitate to do so. However, procedure and standing orders being what they are, it is obvious that only the government can take the appropriate means for making this possible. I, therefore, call on the government to take the necessary steps and follow the suggestion contained in the editorial in the Montreal Star to see that the commissioner, who has rendered such loyal and faithful service and who resigned on a matter of principle-as I indicated it took courage to resign on a matter of principle-does not suffer as a result of his action. I would urge the government to take the necessary steps to avoid punishing a civil servant and to see that he does not suffer any financial loss because he has performed his duty. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that the entire country would welcome such a suggestion.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would he explain exactly what the monetary loss would be if Commissioner Nichlson retires at this time as he wishes?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have not checked the figures, but I am prepared to accept-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Have you any idea what his pension will be?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have not checked the figures, but even if it were only $10 the amount is not important. I do not see why the hon. member quibbles about this. I think it is a sensible suggestion by the Montreal Star. I think the entire country would accede to it, and I certainly feel that a bill or a resolution introduced by the government to restore the commissioner's pension would be well deserved.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit another question? Would he like this resolution put forward before he has this full inquiry he asks for?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the hon. member suggests that such a resolution be considered after a full inquiry, I would go along with that. I would have no objection if the government waited before introducing such a resolution until after the inquiry. Mr. Speaker, I again submit that the proposition made by this newspaper should not be considered adversely

by any of the parties in this house, unless the inquiry discloses things which the country does not yet know. But if we are to accept what we now know, we have the splendid reputation of the commissioner himself and the courage which he showed in resigning one year before he became entitled to a full pension. All these facts in themselves are commendable and should certainly be accepted and considered by every hon. member in this house.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does the hon. member from Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) think that the head of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, which is in fact a semi-military force, is right in his decision to disagree publicly with his superiors?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would love to answer that question, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member has himself pointed out that there is some suspicion that the situation is not clear. Therefore I suggest this inquiry. Certainly if the commissioner resigned because he said, "I could not accept the decision of the minister"-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The decision of his superiors.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was not a decision.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
