subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. I regret to inform the hon. member and those who would ask further questions that the hon. member's time has expired.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before proceeding with my remarks I wish to refer to a statement made this afternoon by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) concerning the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan). I was here in the chamber when the minister made his remarks which were referred to, as reported at page 2624 of Hansard of April 13, 1959. These remarks did not seem to me to carry the meaning attributed to them by the hon. member for Essex East and were in fact delivered in a jocular manner. I want to make it clear that I cannot subscribe to any double standard of public morality or different degrees of sanctity concerning promises. I am quite sure the hon. minister did not intend to give this impression, but since that has been inferred in statements made this afternoon I do not want to let it pass without stating that I do not subscribe to any such theory.

For the past several days we have heard discussions on all topics in connection with the budget. We have listened to discussions about taxation, inflation and other matters. I would like to take this opportunity to discuss a few matters which I believe deserve more serious attention by the government than has heretofore been given. The first subject I want to refer to concerns the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. I feel this department should be among the very first which requires attention. The work of the department, particularly the technical surveys, forms the very basis and beginning of our development program. It is and has been for many years a neglected department. We have been talking big for a long time about our resources in Canada, and I feel we must do something big. Mr. Speaker, scientific research must precede development. We must have geological surveys, magnetic surveys and gravity surveys to determine what is underneath the surface of this country. We must probe the depths of the ocean and find the continental shelf boundaries. We must translate our findings into maps. We must know what we have to develop before we can start to develop it.
What is the situation which we now find? First, the department in understaffed in all its scientific branches. Scientists are so underpaid that they are leaving the government service for industry, for other countries, and even for the universities which have long been classed as providing poorly paid jobs. Even our universities are stealing scientists from the government service. We need grants for scientific research. We need special assistance for those students who have shown some indication of being able to perform those services which are most essential to us if we are going to develop this country to its maximum degree. Mr. Speaker, accommodation is short in all the branches of this department, and although a large building project is under way the buildings not yet completed are now inadequate to serve as a preliminary foundation for the development of our resources in Canada. Even at the dominion observatory here in Ottawa there is such a shortage of space that the scientists are working in the basement of the residence occupied by the dominion astronomer. Too little attention has been given to this problem. More and more the eyes of the public have been directed to our great natural resources.
Our Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton), a great enthusiast for this national development, must have before him the surveys and the maps which will assist in such a development. We have to recognize that this department must
The Budget-Mr. Aiken be properly equipped in order to be able to carry out its researches. This has not been done, and it should be done to a much greater extent. It is realized that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has problems, and they are grave ones. He has brought forward a budget which has very well satisfied the problems that do exist. However, with regard to geological surveys, for example-surveys of the surface and what lies under the surface of our country-only $3,500,000 of the whole national budget is used for this purpose. That is only $1 in every $1,600.
I should now like to turn to a second subject which is always a favourite of mine and one which is related very much to the same type of thing. It concerns the tourist industry in Canada. This is another area where we could be making a great advance. As I have mentioned previously, there can be no argument about the fact that the tourist industry is one of the largest sources of foreign currency available to us. The Canadian government travel bureau is doing an excellent job on the funds which have been allotted to it, and these funds have, in fact, been increased, but I think this house should consider setting up immediately a joint committee on travel in co-operation with the other place, because this has become a neglected field in Canada. It is true that the provincial governments are doing their best, but I think that a greater push is needed from this government. Last session I brought forward a resolution with reference to loans to tourist operators. That subject was very well discussed and I do not intend to raise it again at this time except to say that any project or any idea which can be brought forward to further the encouragement of visitors to this country is one which might well engage the attention of the government.
Tourism should go hand in hand with the development of the country. This is well recognized by the fact that the Canadian government travel bureau is set up within the department of northern affairs. By and large, a lot of our neighbours to the south seem to have the feeling that Canada is the poor man's vacation land. We are somewhat modest in our publicity and careful in our expenditure. That is easy to understand. Mr. Leo Dolan, who was formerly head of the travel bureau, said recently that Canada lacks "snob appeal" for its visitors and suggested that we should rectify this. Just what he meant is hard to pin down, but the general idea is that we must get over the belief that we cannot compete with Europe in connection with our tourist industry.
Here in Canada we have some most interesting tours, and they are improving and increasing with the development of the northland.

The Budget-Mr. Aiken I feel that we must make an effort along these lines of a magnitude that has not heretofore been undertaken. In 1958 there was more travel in Canada than there was in the previous year but this travel was not undertaken by visitors; it was done by more Canadian people travelling between their own province and another province. The influx of tourists from the United States fell off last year, and a number of reasons are given for this-the recession in the United States, the weather, strikes and European competition.
I think the government is doing an excellent job in advertising Canada, but I think we should do more than put advertisements in newspapers and publications. I think we must have publicity agents, people who will bring to visitors from other countries details of the tours and other items that we can provide for them which are of interest and which will provide real competition to European centres.
I should like to speak on a third subject which is related to the other two. This has to do with the fantastic development in North America, and particularly in Canada, over the last few years of pleasure boating. In 1958 over three million Canadians took to the water in pleasure boats. Over 750,000 pleasure boats are now owned by Canadians. The reason for this is that there is a desire to get off the travelled highways and escape the overcrowded conditions that obtain on the highways. Many want to get off the highways and get to more quiet places where they can enjoy a vacation. I think this feeling has been best expressed in an article in Western Business and Industry in which a boating enthusiast has stated:
After being cooped up in an office or driving over jammed highways you discover a completely new world. There is sunshine, space, waves, wind and freedom from worry. I am a different man when I am out there. I am relaxed. I cannot even remember my phone number. A lot of pleasure boat owners agree with me. They have spent time on the open road. They have also spent an irritating portion of that time going ten yards every three minutes, breathing gas fumes and placating the children in the back seat.
Hon. members may wonder what this has to do with the budget, Mr. Speaker. It is just this: I think the government must recognize that facilities for this pleasure boating must be provided. It is a source of income. It is a commercial undertaking just as much as any other. The Department of Public Works, in providing navigation facilities, docks and so forth, and the Department of Transport are both responsible for navigation but I fear that in the past this work has been viewed from the standpoint of commercial navigation. I think we must not lose track of the fact that there is this great swing toward pleasure boating and that the departments


must now take into consideration the provision of facilities for small boats as well as for large ones. I hope that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) will take note of this important new water traffic. At this point I should like to mention the pamphlet "Safety Afloat" put out by the Department of Transport. This has provided an excellent service for those who engage in pleasure boating. It has been well received and well distributed throughout Canada.
In a riding such as mine which is mostly engaged in the tourist business the maintenance of water facilities is particularly important. Many of the standards now set up by the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport are those based on so-called commercial navigation. In fact, nothing is so commercially valuable to the country, I believe, as the pleasure boating traffic which is now developing.
I should like to ask the Department of Public Works to re-examine its policy in relation to the building of docks and navigation facilities. I have to admit that the Minister of Public Works has been extremely cooperative in this regard but always, of course, with a considerable amount of urging on the part of everyone concerned. The district engineer for my area who operates out of Toronto has been extremely understanding in the situation. In the area I represent it is now necessary to have a government official to look after the navigation facilities on behalf of the two departments of government.
Related closely to this is the next and final subject with which I shall deal. It is also connected with boating. I have reference to the Trent canal system. I should like for a few moments to read from a booklet published by the Department of Transport and entitled, "The Trent Canal System," because it is something not sufficiently publicized:
The term "Trent canal" is applied to that series of rivers and lakes which, by a system of dams, locks, short artificial channels and two marine railways, provides 8-foot navigation for 89 miles from lake Ontario to Peterborough and 6-foot navigation for an additional 135 miles to Swift Rapids as well as for 8 miles from Georgian Bay to Big Chute.
The canal began in a small way in 1833 with the construction of a few locks on the Trent and Otonabee rivers and on the Kawartha lakes in order to connect up the small pioneer settlements along their banks and shores. In addition to performing this vital service, these early locks and dams, assisted by an extensive system of log slides, contributed for many years to the flourishing lumber trade of the district. With the depletion of the forests, however, traffic began to settle down to a more prosaic freight-carrying trade. Good roads and motor transport made some inroads on this traffic during the nineteen twenties and thirties, but they have also brought about a

very extensive development of the route as a holiday and tourist playground in which the canal facilities play no inconsiderable part.
I understand that the Department of Transport is now after many years actually considering improving the facilities on the Trent canal. A great number of small craft from both the United States and Canada use the canal extensively for pleasure boating. This brings tourists right into the heart of Ontario with the attendant benefits of purchasing power, the purchases of supplies of fuel and food and other things. I am glad to see that the Department of Transport is now taking an interest in the canal and recognizes that there is an upsurge of interest in pleasure boating that will be with us for many years if highway traffic continues to expand as it has done over the past few years.
Related to the Trent canal system is a dream that has been in existence for fifty years. That is the dream of some day connecting the Trent canal system with the Muskoka lakes. These lakes provide a large inland waterway extending over many miles of lakes and rivers. If the Trent canal system were connected, which would be a comparatively easy and certainly a feasible operation, it would bring to the centre of this country large and small pleasure boats from all parts of the North American continent. There is an easily accessible route through the Morrison lakes and various other lakes leading into lake Muskoka itself. It is hoped that the planners in the Department of Transport will see the value of this dream and make it a reality, thereby providing in the very heart of this country boating facilities that will be equalled by none elsewhere in the world.
I had a number of other matters to mention in connection with the budget but not related to the subjects I have mentioned and for that reason I shall leave them for discussion on a later occasion.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may I should like to refer very briefly to something that was said a little earlier this evening by the shorter member for Halifax (Mr. Morris). I am sorry to observe that the hon. member was called from the chamber. I was rather surprised to hear the congenial and usually Canadian-minded hon. member object quite strenuously to a project which I have had very close to my heart for some considerable time. I refer to the construction of the Richelieu seaway which would join the St. Lawrence river at Sorel to permit travel up the Richelieu river to Lake Champlain and down the Hudson river to New York. I have had the
The Budget-Mr. Cardin opportunity of studying the effects of this project and am convinced that this seaway would be of invaluable economic use not only to the Richelieu valley or to the province of Quebec but to the country as a whole.
I feel sure the hon. member does not wish to impede or provide obstacles to economic improvement anywhere in the country just as other hon. members of this house are always pleased to learn of projects that are of assistance to the maritime provinces. Indeed, in this respect although hon. gentlemen opposite do not always agree with me I feel that at least some members of the Conservative party would agree that this seaway from the St. Lawrence to New York through the Richelieu river would be of invaluable economic assistance.
I should now like to come to a detailed consideration of the budget. I believe it is quite clear that the budget brought down some weeks ago is symptomatic of a very marked and serious lack of administrative responsibility. To my mind the record deficit with which the country is now burdened for the most part is due to the fact that political expediency and opportunism have replaced the objectivity and the realism which are essential in a government which intends to administer in the interest of the country's welfare. Because of the necessity of having in Canada responsible governmental administration if we are to achieve the highest summit of prosperity which our labour force, our industrial power and our natural resources warrant, and because we are now faced with this budget, with the staggering results of a most disquieting political philosophy, I think it would be extremely useful for us to reflect seriously on the often-quoted words of Thomas Jefferson on public spending. May I quote Thomas Jefferson as follows:
I place economy among the most Important virtues and public debt as the greatest of dangers to be feared. To preserve our independence, we must not allow our leaders to load us with perpetual debt. We must make our choice between economy with liberty, or profusion with servitude.
These words are as fundamentally true today as they were generations ago, and in spite of the Utopian promises and commitments of the Conservative party in 1957, the huge record deficit that we have in front of us today brings us back to the cold, hard realization that no one really gets anything for nothing. As a matter of fact there seems to be a natural law which inflicts the loss of independence, of pride and of liberty on all those who try to obtain something for nothing. In this case, along with those losses, Canada has been inflicted with a huge deficit, an increased national debt and increased taxation.

The Budget-Mr. Cardin
It might also be well to reflect on a paragraph which appears in the final edition of the Gordon commission report, found at page 14, and I quote:
There will be plenty of ways to spend our increasing national wealth. We will first have to meet the claims of defence and decide what we are prepared to pay as our contribution to the collective military force of the western world designed to deter an atomic attack. We may also want to round out our social security program and to increase the payments made under it. There will also be proposals for expenditures on projects to add ease and grace to our common life and on other projects that would contribute either directly or indirectly to our economic growth. But we must recognize that these claims are all competing. At any one time we may have to decide that some of them are beyond our present means and have to be deferred. For if they were accepted indiscriminately and all superimposed on the normal operations of the economy, the result might well be an inflation that would bear cruelly on some groups in the community and that would price us out of some of the world markets in which we must compete. If that were to happen, we might wake up to find that our prodigality had cost us dear.
Mr. Speaker, our prodigality has indeed cost us dearly, with the huge deficit of $617 million, and the people of Canada are now asked to pay for the lack of foresight and the lack of wisdom in this government's administration. No one, not even my socialist friends to my right, not having the responsibility of administration, claimed, as indeed did the Conservatives in 1957, that they had a magic formula that would make of Canada a Utopian paradise. There is no one, there is no government, who can return to the people more in the way of social or national security than is warranted by the moneys which the people themselves have contributed to the common fund and for a common good. I submit it is an irresponsible government which commits itself, as this government has done, to the expenditure of moneys which it knows surpasses the capacity of the people to pay and which in this case has resulted in a huge deficit and increased taxation for the people of Canada. And what for, Mr. Speaker? In order to create, and for the sole purpose of creating, the impression that this government was indeed fulfilling the irrational, exaggerated and contradictory promises it made in 1957.
While we study the deficit and note the deficit for this year as well as an estimated deficit of some $400 million for next year, in spite of the increased taxes across the board, I could not help and I still cannot help but hear ringing in my ears the echoes of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Diefenbaker) most theatrical voice when he shouted from one coast to the other of this country that the Liberals had a surplus of some $500 million;
[Mr. Cardin.1
that the Liberals were overtaxing the Canadian people by $150 per family per year; when he shouted from coast to coast that the government at Ottawa was rich and the provinces and the municipalities were poor. If those accusations were true, then I accuse the government of having within 20 months squandered all that wealth without having one trace of it in any of the government records. If the accusations were not true, then I accuse the government of having used electoral tactics which in fact undermined the very concept we have of our democratic form of government.
If we have come to the point in the evolution of our political life where the winning of elections is the sole consideration of a political party and where half-truths and untruths are asserted as facts, and where impossible and unrealizable projects are presented to the Canadian public not only as being desirable but as being economically and constitutionally sound when they are not, then I submit, that such tactics will destroy the country's faith in our parliamentary system. They will destroy the country's faith in our public men and in fact they will make out of our parliamentary system a veritable farce. They will keep away sincere, honest and independent young men from political life and leave the future generations of Canada a prey to the most unscrupulous and obnoxious form of dictatorship and government banditism.
Lest anyone should believe that the cause of my fears are unfounded I would ask hon. members to compare the speeches that were made by the Conservative party in the election of 1957 with this budget, the results of the administration of 20 months of Conservative rule. I would ask hon. members to take a look also at the statement which was made by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) the other evening, which is to be found at page 2624 of Hansard. In order to be fair to the minister I am going to quote the whole paragraph:
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that promises of any kind, whether pre-election promises or otherwise, should be honoured and respected so far as circumstances will possibly permit, but I would suggest to you, sir-and I think all hon. members on both sides of the house would accept this general principle-that promises made to this House of Commons and promises made to parliament stand in an even more favoured position in so far as sanctity and respect are concerned than promises made during an election campaign.
As the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) said this afternoon, we do not accept the general principle of the Minister of National Revenue. We feel very strongly that statements and promises made concerning

the administration of this country to the people of Canada by our public men must be as respected and as sacred as statements and promises made in this house. The statement of the Minister of National Revenue is not only an indescribable insult to the intelligence and dignity of the Canadian people but is a formal denial of the basic concept of democracy. How can the people of Canada have faith in our public men? How can they choose wisely the administrators of the country when in fact the Minister of National Revenue, a minister of this government, states that what is said in the house is more sacred than what is said elsewhere to the people who in fact chose those who sit in this house and who act on behalf of the people of Canada?
We have heard a great deal about the dignity, respect and rights of parliament, and they must be maintained. I submit they can be maintained only if first of all we respect and acknowledge the rights, privileges and prerogatives of the Canadian electorate. The Minister of National Revenue has indeed confirmed the dangers we have seen in the political attitude of the government and he has corroborated better than anyone else possibly could have the accusations we have been levelling against the government that it has indeed ignored the elementary rights of the Canadian electorate and that as a matter of fact it has trampled on the dignity of the Canadian people in its haste to achieve power.
Today the government's defence of this abominable budget is that under the circumstances the government had no other alternative but to increase taxes. Mr. Speaker, that is begging the question. The point of argument is that the government is responsible for the circumstances in which the country now finds itself. It is the attitude,
The Budget-Mr. Cardin policies and actions of the government which, in the space of 20 months, have brought about a deterioration in economic conditions and the financial position of the country whereby we have passed from a surplus of $257 million in 1957 to a deficit of $617 million in 1959 and an estimated deficit of $400 million in 1960.
If Canadians today are being burdened with increased taxation without seeing the possibility of relief in the immediate future, it is not only because the government has demonstrated the attitude of immaturity to be found in that type of person who continually over-tips without being able to afford it but also because the government is caught in the web of words and promises it wove in order to win the election. In order to save face as much as possible and in order not to be laughed right out of parliament the government has implemented a fraction of the irresponsible promises it made and as a result it has jeopardized our economic position and has imposed additional tax burdens on the Canadian people. As we look at the deficit and prepare to take additional money out of our pockets to pay increased taxes we may well ask ourselves, what has the government done, what has the government returned to the people to justify or even explain the huge deficit with which we are now confronted? What has the government to show for record peacetime expenditures?
I am entering on a new subject, Mr. Speaker, and I wonder whether I might call it ten o'clock?
